ranges.en: Beit Shammai rule that an egg laid on a Festival may be eaten that same day.
Beit Hillel rule that an egg laid on a Festival may not be eaten.
Beit Shammai: leaven is forbidden at an olive-sized measure, while edible leavened bread needs a larger date-sized measure.
Beit Hillel: the same olive-sized measure applies to both leaven and leavened bread.
Introduces the case of someone slaughtering a wild animal or bird on a Festival.
Beit Shammai: one digs with a shovel and covers the blood with the earth dug up.
Beit Hillel: slaughter is forbidden unless covering earth was prepared before the Festival began.
Both schools agree that after slaughter one digs and covers, and that a prepared stove's ashes suffice.
Asks which case the mishna is actually addressing.
Proposes that the mishna refers to a chicken kept for eating.
Asks why Beit Hillel forbid under that reading, since the egg is merely a detached part of food.
Proposes the alternative reading: a chicken kept for laying eggs.
Asks Beit Shammai's reason; since the egg is muktze, what is the difficulty?
Suggests Beit Shammai may not hold the muktze prohibition at all, dissolving the difficulty.
Assumes that whoever permits muktze must also forbid objects that came into being on the Festival.
Asks again what Beit Shammai's reason is, given that assumption.
Rav Naḥman: Beit Shammai follow R. Shimon (no muktze), Beit Hillel follow R. Yehuda (muktze applies).
Challenges whether Rav Naḥman really said that Beit Hillel follow R. Yehuda.
Cites a mishna where Beit Shammai permit removing muktze bones and Beit Hillel forbid it, contrary to that assignment.
Rav Naḥman replies that the mishna's version is not halakha and only the reversed assignment is valid.
Answers that the unattributed Shabbat mishna reflects R. Shimon's view, which is the accepted halakha.
Quotes the Shabbat mishna permitting pumpkins and carcasses to be cut before animals, as R. Shimon holds.
Concludes that Beit Hillel are read as following R. Shimon, qualified by the word 'however'.

ranges.en: States that the Festival teaching is an unattributed mishna that follows Rabbi Yehuda.
Cites the mishna forbidding chopping wood from prepared construction beams or a beam broken on a Festival.
Restates Rav Naḥman's reading that Beit Hillel follow R. Yehuda, who prohibits muktze.
Premise identifying Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi as the editor who formulated the anonymous mishnayot.
Asks why the anonymous Shabbat ruling follows R. Shimon while the Festival ruling follows R. Yehuda.
Shabbat is strict, so the lenient view is used to avoid contempt; Festival is lenient, so the stringent view is used.
Asks how the mishna was ultimately explained, and why the dispute is over the egg rather than the chicken.
The egg is used to highlight the far-reaching leniency of Beit Shammai, who permit even this item.
Objects that the dispute should instead be framed over the chicken, to show Beit Hillel's stringency, or over both.
Proposes a hypothetical mishna wording covering the chicken and its eggs, with Shammai permitting and Hillel forbidding.
Rabba's alternative: the case is a chicken kept for eating and an egg laid on a Festival after Shabbat, so preparation is the issue.
Rabba holds that an egg laid today was already fully formed yesterday and only emerged today.
Notes that Rabba consistently applies this reasoning about preparation for Shabbat and Festival.
Asks what the verse about preparing for the manna actually teaches.
Quotes Exodus 16:5 about preparing on the sixth day, the verse Rabba relies on.
Derives from the verse that weekdays may prepare for Shabbat or a Festival, but Shabbat and Festival may not prepare for each other.
Abaye objects: if the concern is only preparation, an ordinary Festival's egg should be permitted.
Rabba replies that the egg is forbidden only by rabbinic decree, due to a Festival that falls after Shabbat.
Abaye asks whether an ordinary Shabbat's egg should likewise be permitted, provided it is not cooked.
Rabba similarly responds that the decree applies because of a Shabbat that falls after a Festival.
Abaye challenges whether a preventive decree of this kind is actually issued at all.
Cites a baraita: a chicken slaughtered on a Festival with fully formed eggs inside may be eaten that day.
If such decrees exist, the Sages should have prohibited those internal eggs, which resemble eggs laid that day.
Rabba replies that the Sages decree only for common cases, not rare ones like fully formed eggs inside a hen.
Rav Yosef gives a different reason: a decree based on fruits that fall from a tree on Shabbat or Festival.
Abaye asks Rav Yosef what the reason is for the decree concerning fallen fruits.

ranges.en: Rav Yosef's reason for fallen fruit: a decree lest one climb the tree and pick it, which is a form of harvesting.
Objects: shall we issue a decree in order to prevent the violation of another decree?
Replies that all these prohibitions are components of one original decree, so the objection does not apply.
Rabbi Yitzḥak's alternative: the egg is prohibited as a decree against liquid that seeped from fruit on a Festival.
Abaye asks the reason for prohibiting liquid that seeped from fruit.
Explains it as a decree lest one deliberately squeeze the fruit, which would constitute threshing.
Objects again: shall we decree a decree to guard against violating another decree?
Yitzḥak replies that all these prohibitions form one decree, so the egg falls under the same rule.
Observes that none of these explanations follow Rav Naḥman's view, and the others reject Rabba's preparation-based reasoning.
Asks why Rav Yosef, whose explanation resembles Rabbi Yitzḥak's, did not adopt that explanation.
Rav Yosef could say an egg is food like fallen fruit, which excludes juice as drink not comparable to an egg.
Asks the reverse: why did Rabbi Yitzḥak not adopt Rav Yosef's explanation?
An egg is enclosed in the hen as juice is enclosed in fruit, a closer comparison than fallen fruit exposed on the tree.
Rabbi Yoḥanan also holds that the egg prohibition is a decree on liquid that seeped from fruit.
Shows Rabbi Yoḥanan resolving a contradiction between two of Rabbi Yehuda's statements in a way that reveals his own view.
Cites a mishna: liquid squeezed from fruit is forbidden, and Rabbi Yehuda permits it only from fruit meant for eating.
Infers that Rabbi Yehuda holds all food emerging from food is food that was separated, not a new food.
Raises a contradiction from another statement of Rabbi Yehuda.
Cites Rabbi Yehuda on untithed fruit stipulations over two Festival days, applying the same logic to an egg laid on the first day.
Notes that this rule seems to contradict Rabbi Yehuda's earlier view that such emergence is merely separation.
Rabbi Yoḥanan resolves it by reversing the attribution of the second-day opinions, so Rabbi Yehuda stays consistent.
Concludes that the egg and seeped liquid share one reason: a rabbinic decree against liquid that oozed from fruit.

ranges.en: Ravina's alternative: do not reverse the views; Rabbi Yehuda was speaking in line with the Rabbis' position.
Recasts Rabbi Yehuda's view as permitting the egg even on the first day, and proposes conceding the second day as a separate sanctity.
The Rabbis reject the concession: the two Festival days form one sanctity, so the doubt applies to both.
Ravina son of Rav Ulla: the case is a chicken kept for laying, and Rabbi Yehuda, who holds muktze, applies his view there.
Raises an objection from a baraita.
Baraita: eggs laid on Shabbat or a Festival are muktze and cannot be moved, though a vessel may cover them; mixtures remain forbidden.
Explains the baraita under Rabba: the prohibition stems from lack of preparation, so the doubt is Torah-level and treated stringently.
Under Rav Yosef and Rabbi Yitzḥak the prohibition is a rabbinic decree, so a doubt about it is treated leniently.
Answers that the latter clause concerns a possibly tereifa chicken, so the doubt is about its status rather than Festival status.
Objects: a Festival doubt is temporary and not nullified, but a tereifa doubt would be nullified by majority, conflicting with the baraita.
Proposes that eggs are significant and not nullified, which fits the view that items sometimes counted are significant.
Objects that this works only for the view that always-counted items are significant; what is the answer for that view?
Cites the Orla mishna: mixed bundles of vineyard crops must all be burned per R. Meir, while the Rabbis allow nullification at one in two hundred.
Continues the mishna: R. Meir treats counted items as significant; the Rabbis list six such items, and R. Akiva adds more.
Notes which prohibitions apply to these items: orla for some, and diverse kinds of vineyard crops for others.
Records the amoraic dispute: R. Yoḥanan limits significance to always-counted items, while R. Shimon ben Lakish includes any item sometimes counted.
Objects: the egg solution works for R. Shimon ben Lakish, but for R. Yoḥanan eggs are not significant and should be nullified.
Rav Pappa: R. Yoḥanan's view fits the tanna of the dried-fig litra, who holds counted items cannot be nullified even if rabbinic.
Cites the mishna on a litra of dried figs with uncertain tithing, and the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer about the pressed figs.

ranges.en: One tanna holds that upper fig circles are treated as separate pieces, while the tithed lower circles nullify them.
R. Yehoshua: with a hundred vessel mouths present the prohibited litra is nullified; otherwise the mouths are forbidden and the bottoms permitted.
R. Yehuda reports R. Eliezer's view: a hundred permitted mouths nullify the litra; otherwise the mouths are forbidden and the bottoms permitted.
R. Yehoshua: even three hundred mouths cannot nullify this litra, which can never be nullified.
States that all agree a fig cake pressed into a vessel of unknown location is nullified.
Asks whether all really agree, since that is the very point under dispute.
Rav Pappa explains: the unknown spot was north or south of the circle, so all agree the litra is nullified.
Rav Ashi: the doubt is Festival versus weekday, so it is temporary and cannot be nullified, even when rabbinic.
Baraita: Aḥerim cite R. Eliezer that an egg laid on a Festival may be eaten along with its mother.
Asks which case the baraita is addressing.
Objects: if the hen is kept for food the ruling is trivial; if kept for laying, the mother would also be forbidden.
Rabbi Zeira reads the baraita as meaning the egg is permitted through its mother: if the hen is eaten, so is the egg.
Asks in which circumstances this ruling applies.
Abaye: the hen was bought without a declared purpose, so Festival slaughter retroactively fixes it as food or as an egg-layer.
Rav Mari: the phrase 'it and its mother may be eaten' is an exaggeration for emphasis, not a literal ruling.
Cites another baraita: an egg may be eaten with its mother, and a chick with its shell, the same exaggeration.
Asks what the addition 'and its shell' means.
Objects: if an actual shell is meant, shells are not edible, so the phrase must mean something else.
Proposes a chick still in its shell, where all agree it is forbidden, since the dispute concerns only chicks that have emerged.
Concludes that 'a chick and its shell' is an exaggeration, just like 'it and its mother,' stressing the egg's permitted status.
Introduces the amoraic dispute: Rav holds an egg laid on Shabbat is forbidden on the Festival, while R. Yoḥanan permits it.
Asks whether Rav's view is that the two days form one continuous sanctity.
Objects: Rav himself ruled like the four elders following R. Eliezer, who treats Shabbat and a Festival as two sanctities.
Resolves that the dispute concerns Rabba's preparation: Rav accepts it as prohibited, while R. Yoḥanan does not.
Presents the parallel tannaitic rule: an egg laid on Shabbat may be eaten on a Festival, and vice versa.
R. Yehuda, citing R. Eliezer, says the matter is still disputed, as the Shammai-Hillel debate shows.
Cites Beit Shammai permitting and Beit Hillel forbidding an egg on the day it was laid, as evidence of the dispute.
Narrative: Rav Adda bar Ahava's host had eggs laid on a Festival before Shabbat and came to consult him.
The host asks whether the eggs may be roasted now on the Festival and eaten tomorrow, once the prohibition lapses.
Rav Adda: even under R. Yoḥanan, such eggs may be swallowed raw only the next day, not moved or roasted on the day laid.
Cites a baraita: eggs laid on Shabbat or a Festival may not be moved, even to cover a vessel or support a bed.
Narrative: a man came to Rav Pappa with eggs laid on Shabbat before a Festival, asking whether they may be eaten.
Asks whether these eggs may be eaten tomorrow on the Festival.
Rav Pappa tells him to leave now and return tomorrow.
Explains the reason: Rav feared drunkenness during Festival meals, so he did not rule that day; the man returned the next day.

ranges.en: Recalls that had he ruled then he would have said the eggs are permitted, following the principle that halakha follows R. Yoḥanan over Rav.
Rava: the halakha follows Rav in these three cases, whether the ruling is lenient or stringent.
R. Yoḥanan rules that branches fallen from a palm on Shabbat may not be kindled on the Festival.
Explains the difference: an egg fit for swallowing is still forbidden on its day, while branches could be wrongly permitted that day.
Rav Mattana: branches falling into an oven on a Festival may be kindled together with wood prepared the day before.
Objects: doesn't he turn over prohibited wood while cooking?
Since most of the wood is permitted, turning it over means turning permitted wood; the prohibited part is nullified by the majority.
Objects: doesn't he nullify a prohibited item ab initio, which the mishna forbids?
Only Torah-level prohibitions cannot be nullified ab initio; rabbinic ones, such as muktze, may be nullified.
Asks how Rav Ashi's principle, that rabbinic prohibitions cannot be nullified, fits this case.
Replies that the principle applies only while the prohibited item is intact; here the wood is already charcoal.
Records the amoraic dispute on the Diaspora Festival days: Rav permits an egg laid on one day on the other, Rav Asi prohibits it.
Objects: if Rav Asi holds the two days are one sanctity, why did he recite havdala between them?
Rav Asi was uncertain about the ordinance, so he acted stringently both in the egg ruling and in reciting havdala.
Rabbi Zeira holds with Rav Asi: the two days are one sanctity, not an uncertainty-based custom, since the calendar is now fixed.
Abaye: it is more reasonable to follow Rav, since the second day is kept because of uncertainty.
Cites the Rosh HaShana mishna: after Samaritan interference, messengers were sent, and distant places kept a second day from uncertainty.
Infers from the mishna that without Samaritan interference, or with timely messengers, only one day would be observed.
Asks why two days are still observed in the Diaspora, now that the calendar is fixed and known.
Eretz Yisrael sent a warning to keep the ancestral custom, since monarchic decrees might disrupt the calendar and cause later confusion.
Rav and Shmuel both hold that an egg laid on one Rosh HaShana day is prohibited on the other, given the special status of those days.
Cites the Rosh HaShana mishna about witnesses who arrived late to testify on the new moon, which bears on the two days' status.

ranges.en: The Levites' confusion led the court to accept Rosh HaShana witnesses only until the afternoon offering time.
Witnesses arriving after the afternoon offering make both that day and the following day sacred.
Rabba states that after Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's ordinance, an egg laid on one Rosh HaShana day is permitted the next.
A Mishnah cited as support, recording Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's post-Temple ordinance restoring all-day acceptance of testimony.
Abaye objects that Rav and Shmuel both held that such an egg is prohibited.
Rabba replies that he quotes Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, while Abaye quotes the later authorities Rav and Shmuel.
The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah contradicts the position of Rav and Shmuel.
The Mishnah's ruling applies to Eretz Yisrael, while the Babylonian rule applies to Diaspora Jews who keep two days.
Rav Yosef holds that even after the ordinance, the egg remains prohibited.
The Gemara asks the reason for Rav Yosef's position.
A prohibition established by vote requires a second vote to lift it, even once its reason has lapsed.
Rav Yosef asks from where he derives his position.
Deuteronomy 5:26, return to your tents, is read as referring to wives, supporting Rav Yosef's view.
Exodus 19:13 shows that the prohibition at Sinai was explicitly lifted by a formal sounding of the horn.
A baraita on a fourth-year vineyard and the boundaries of Jerusalem's environs for second-tithe redemption.
Ulla, or per another version Rabba bar bar Hana, reports Rabbi Yochanan's teaching.
Asks the reason the Sages required fruit from Jerusalem's environs to be brought to Jerusalem.
To beautify Jerusalem's markets with an abundance of fruit.
A baraita on Rabbi Eliezer's vineyard near Lod, which lies within Jerusalem's environs for this halakha.

ranges.en: Rabbi wished to make the fruit ownerless for the poor, but his students said his colleagues had already permitted it.
Asks who the colleagues are who had voted.
The colleagues are Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai and the court that took the vote.
A formal vote was needed to lift the decree, which shows an egg prohibition was never lifted by vote.
Asks what the words and it says are introducing.
It means Rav Yosef is saying the following.
Exodus 19:15 says to be ready for three days and avoid women, so the restriction would lapse by itself after three days.
Deuteronomy 5:30 says to return to your tents, which the Gemara reads as an explicit permission to go home.
Asks why the second verse is needed at all.
Concludes that any matter established by vote requires another vote to permit it.
Objects that the return to tents only meant marital relations were a mitzva, so the verse proves nothing.
Brings Exodus 19:13 about the ram's horn, which shows explicit permission was needed for ascent.
Challenges that Exodus 34:3 shows the prohibition ends right after revelation, making the horn verse unnecessary.
Asks why the horn verse is needed if the other verse suffices.
Concludes again that a vote-established matter needs another vote to permit it.
Objects that this applies only to Torah law, not to rabbinic prohibitions.
Brings a baraita on a fourth-year vineyard whose rabbinic status was lifted by a vote.
Suggests Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai also voted to permit eggs, as a parallel case.
Explains the vote concerned testimony about the new moon, not eggs, so eggs were not voted on.
Abaye objects that an egg's status follows testimony, so no separate vote on eggs is needed.
Rav Adda and Rav Shalman hold that even after the ordinance, an egg remains prohibited.
Asks the reason for their position.
Fear that people will eat eggs as before, not realizing the two-day sanctity has become one.
Challenges that by the same logic testimony should not be accepted either.
Asks the difference between the two cases.
Testimony is entrusted to the court, which can distinguish decree reasons, while eggs are public and need caution.
Rava says the same: even after the ordinance, an egg remains prohibited.
Rava argues Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai concedes both days remain sacred, proving that the two days form one sanctity.
Rava concludes the halakha follows Rav in these three cases, whether lenient or stringent.

ranges.en: Rava rules that a body dying on a festival's second day is attended to by Jews, and the Rosh HaShana egg rule is stricter.
The Neharde'a Sages hold that even an egg is permitted on the second Rosh HaShana day, like other festivals.
Asks what the Neharde'a Sages are thinking, meaning what concern they have.
The concern is that witnesses may not arrive, so the court might make Elul a full thirty-day month.
Cites Rav that since Ezra, Elul was never full, so Rosh HaShana always falls on the thirtieth day.
Mar Zutra: the burial may be attended on the second day only when the body's delay risks decay.
Rav Ashi: even if not delayed, a burial on the day of death is not attended to on the festival.
Asks the reason for Rav Ashi's ruling.
The Sages equated the second festival day with a weekday for the dead, permitting cutting a cloak and myrtles.
Ravina: nowadays, with the habarei, this leniency must be curtailed, so the dead are not buried on that day.
Ravina sees Rav Ashi sad during the Rosh HaShana festival days.
Ravina asks why the Master is sad.
Rav Ashi explains he failed to prepare an eruv tavshilin for Shabbat.
Ravina asks why Rav Ashi does not prepare the eruv tavshilin today.
Rava permits preparing an eruv tavshilin from one diaspora festival day to the next, under a stipulated condition.
Rav Ashi objects that Rava's ruling concerned diaspora festivals, not the two days of Rosh HaShana.
Ravina replies that Neharde'a permits eggs on Rosh HaShana's second day, so the same should apply to food.
Rav Mordekhai objects that Rav Ashi explicitly rejected the Neharde'a view on this issue.
Rav and Shmuel, or Rabbi Yochanan, dispute whether a chick hatched on a festival is prohibited.
Rav: it is muktze and prohibited; Shmuel or Rabbi Yochanan: hatching makes it fit for slaughter, so it is permitted.
Rav Kahana and Rav Asi ask what distinguishes this from a calf born on a festival.
Rav replies that a calf is prepared through its mother's slaughter, so it was never muktze.
Rav Kahana and Rav Ashi challenge him with a calf of a tereifa mother, which may be slaughtered on a festival.
Rav was silent and did not answer.
Rabba, or per another version Rav Yosef, asks why Rav stayed silent.
A calf of a tereifa is prepared for dogs, so it is not fully muktze, unlike a chick in its shell.
Abaye opens an objection to this explanation, with its content continuing beyond this text.

ranges.en: Food fit for people is not automatically prepared for dogs, as the Gemara states before citing a mishna.
Mishna: carcasses may be cut before dogs on Shabbat, but Rabbi Yehuda forbids a non-carcass that was not dead before Shabbat.
Asks whether food prepared for dogs can be considered prepared for people.
Rav replies that people-fit food is not dog-prepared, but dog-fit food stays in mind as people-fit.
The dispute is supported by two baraitot, one following Rav and another following Shmuel or Rabbi Yochanan.
A baraita following Rav: a calf born on a festival is permitted, but a chick is prohibited.
Asks what distinguishes the calf from the chick.
The calf is prepared through its mother's slaughter, while the chick is not prepared through its mother.
A baraita following Shmuel or Rabbi Yochanan: both a calf and a chick born on a festival are permitted.
Asks the reason for the chick's permission.
The calf is prepared through its mother, while the chick permits itself through slaughter.
A baraita: a chick born on a festival is prohibited.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that even on a weekday such a chick is prohibited, since its eyes are unopened.
Asks in accordance with whose opinion this baraita follows.
It follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, whose view Leviticus 11:42 supports by including unopened chicks among creeping things.
Rav Huna cites Rav: an egg is fully formed upon its emergence from the mother.
Asks what Rav meant by fully formed upon emergence.
Hypothesis: if so, an egg inside its mother is meat and prohibited with milk.
A baraita permits eggs found inside a slaughtered hen to be eaten with milk, contradicting that hypothesis.
Reformulation: an egg is permitted on a festival only if it emerged on a weekday.
Hypothesis: then an egg still inside its mother is prohibited on a festival.
A baraita permits eggs found inside a slaughtered hen to be eaten on a festival, contradicting this.
Proposed reply: the baraita teaches what the mishna omitted, so Rav's ruling is consistent with the mishna.
Mishna: an egg laid on a festival is debated by Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, but eggs still inside are all permitted.
Proposed reply: Beit Hillel forbid eggs inside the mother too, and the mishna's laid wording reflects Beit Shammai's breadth.
A baraita permits eggs found inside a slaughtered hen to be eaten on a festival, refuting that reading.
Asks in accordance with whose opinion this baraita is.
Neither Beit Shammai nor Beit Hillel; it reflects the view that eggs are fully formed upon emergence.
Rav explains that an egg that has emerged can produce chicks, unlike one still inside its mother.
Asks what the practical difference of this distinction is.
It matters for buying and selling.
Gives an illustrative anecdote about a seller addressing customers about eggs; the anecdote continues beyond this text.

ranges.en: Defahya's buyer received eggs of a slaughtered hen; Rabbi Ami ruled the sale void as a mistaken transaction.
Asks whether this ruling is obvious.
Considers the rejected reading that the buyer wanted the eggs for eating rather than for hatching.
Asks the practical difference, meaning what the buyer could claim from the seller.
Rabbi Ami teaches that the sale involved a fundamental error, making it void.
A second case: a buyer asks for rooster eggs, receives eggs absorbed from the ground, and Rabbi Ami voids the sale.
Asks whether that ruling is obvious.
Considers the rejected reading that this buyer wanted the eggs for food, because they are fatter.
Asks the practical difference of this reading.
Teaches that the sale involved a fundamental error and is void.
Offers an alternative reading of Rav's statement: an egg is complete when most of it has emerged.
Cites a baraita of Rabbi Yochanan: an egg mostly emerged before the festival is permitted on the festival.
Another reading: an egg is complete only when all of it has emerged.
Infers that complete emergence is needed, so an egg mostly out is not considered complete.
This reading excludes Rabbi Yochanan's own view, though Rav's statement can still match his.
A baraita: eggs found inside a slaughtered hen are permitted with milk.
Rabbi Yaakov disagrees: eggs still attached by sinews are prohibited with milk, since they count as meat.
Asks who the tanna is who taught this baraita.
The baraita lists pure and impure items from a bird carcass, identifying the source of the teaching.
Asks who taught that a cluster of eggs is pure.
Rav Yosef rules that this is not in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yaakov.
If it were Rabbi Yaakov, he would have said attached eggs are prohibited, showing he treats them as meat.
Abaye objects that Rabbi Yaakov's view may apply only to the milk prohibition, not to impurity.
Abaye adds that impurity should not be extended by a rabbinic stringency, so the view cannot apply to impurity.
Some transmit a different version of the discussion.
Asks who taught that a cluster of eggs from the ovary is impure.
Rav Yosef identifies the source as Rabbi Yaakov, who holds that attached eggs are prohibited.
Abaye asks how we know the cluster refers to these eggs rather than to the ovary itself.
Replies that the ovary is meat but is taught because some people do not eat it, just as with the craw.
Baraita: a species is born by day, by night, or either, according to when it mates; examples are a chicken, a bat and a human.
The Master restates that a species mating by day is born by day, and this is a chicken.
Asks the practical difference of this classification.
Rav Mari son of Rav Kahana: an egg found in the nest the next morning on the festival is permitted.
Objects: did he not check the nest before the festival, so the egg must have been laid on the festival?
Replies that even a careful check does not rule out an egg mostly emerged before the festival, per Rabbi Yochanan.
Asks whether that is so, since Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul reports Rav ruling such an egg prohibited.
Quotes Rav's ruling as reported by Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul: an egg found the next morning is prohibited.
There the case is an egg absorbed from the earth, not produced by male fertilization.
Objects that the same reasoning applies to Rav Mari's case, so the egg could be earth-absorbed.
Ravina says a tradition teaches that wherever a male is present, a hen does not absorb from the earth.
Asks how close a male must be for this rule to apply.
Rav Gamda, in Rav's name, answers that the male may be in any place, the answer continuing beyond this text.

ranges.en: Describes Rav Mari's sixty-house examination and a ruling on whether a hen crosses a river by bridge or by rope.
Asks how Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul's ruling was established.
Asks why the case specifies an examination, since the same ruling should apply without one.
Without an examination the egg may have been laid the previous day, so it is not prohibited.
Objects that if he did examine, the egg may have mostly emerged and returned, per Rabbi Yochanan.
A case of an egg mostly emerged and then returned is rare, so it is assumed not to happen.
Rav's ruling that crushed garlic left uncovered is prohibited due to the danger of snake venom.
Mishna: Beit Shammai set leaven at an olive-bulk and leavened bread at a date-bulk; Beit Hillel use an olive-bulk for both.
Asks the reasoning behind Beit Shammai's position.
Beit Shammai reason that mentioning leaven separately shows its measure differs from that of leavened bread.
Beit Hillel need both terms, since each alone could mislead about the measure for the other.
Asks how Beit Shammai can differ, given Rabbi Zeira's view that leaven equals leavened bread.
Everyone agrees on the eating measure; the dispute concerns removal, with Beit Hillel deriving removal from eating.
Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina says the dispute concerns removal only, while the eating measures are agreed.
Baraita on Exodus 13:7 confirming that the dispute concerns the obligation of removal, not liability for eating.
Mishna: on a festival, slaughtering a wild animal or bird without prepared earth raises a dispute over digging to cover the blood.
Analyzes the mishna's wording to infer that Beit Shammai permit slaughter even ab initio.
Beit Hillel say one may not slaughter and cover the blood; Beit Shammai allow slaughter and covering ab initio.
Objects that Beit Hillel concede covering after the fact, showing the mishna addresses ab initio rather than after-the-fact action.
Rabba's reading: the mishna concerns a person consulting a Sage, and gives the schools' answers to him.
Rav Yosef's alternative reading of the same consultation case.
Abaye asks whether Rav Yosef and Rabba dispute Rabbi Zeira's transmission of Rav.
Rav's ruling, transmitted by Rabbi Zeira: a slaughterer must place earth beneath and above the blood, per Leviticus 17:13.
Abaye suggests Rav Yosef follows Rabbi Zeira and Rabba does not, so digging must come first.
Rav Yosef replies that both follow Rabbi Zeira, and they dispute only the case without prepared earth.
Rabba fears one will reconsider and dig needlessly; Rav Yosef fears people will refrain from rejoicing on the festival.
Mishna: if one slaughtered anyway, Beit Hillel concede he may dig with a spade and cover the blood.
Rabbi Zerika, in Rav Yehuda's name: this holds only if a spade was already embedded in the ground before the festival.
Asks what an embedded spade accomplishes, since crushing the earth is still done on the festival.
Rav Hiyya bar Ashi, in Rav's name, begins an answer about crushing; the answer continues beyond this text.

8a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Clarifies that the earth in the ruling is loose earth that needs no further crushing.
Objects that even loose earth requires making a hole by removing it, which seems to violate the festival.
Rabbi Abba: one who digs a hole on Shabbat without intending a pit is exempt, since the act is destructive.
Mishna: the ashes of a stove are considered prepared for covering blood.
Asks why the mishna suddenly mentions stove ashes, which it never introduced.
Rabba: the tanna means that stove ashes are also prepared, with no need to set them aside the day before.
Rav: stove ashes are prepared only if lit before the festival, and hot ashes fit for roasting an egg are permitted.
A baraita matches this: stove ashes lit before the festival are prepared, while those lit on it are not.
Earth brought into a garden or ruin before the festival may be used to cover blood, and a basketful may serve all needs.
Mar Zutra limits this to earth set aside in a designated corner, which is then intended for all needs.
Objects from a mishna on a koy, whose blood may not be covered, which would conflict with Rav Yehuda's basket-earth ruling.
The mishna refers to a case with no prepared earth at all, so the basket earth in that case is likewise unavailable.
Asks why the case specifies uncertain status, since definitely wild animals may not be slaughtered either.
Uncertainty is different: festival joy permits slaughter, but not covering the blood without prepared earth.

8b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Challenge: the latter clause implies material to cover the blood exists, so why state the prohibition at all?
Rabba answers that stove ash is prepared only for a definite obligation, not for an uncertain one.
Asks the reason why the ash is not considered prepared in an uncertain case.
If making a hole is the reason, a definite case involves a hole too, so the prohibition should apply generally.
Proposed resolution: per Rabbi Abba, making a hole is destructive rather than forbidden labor, so uncertainty is unproblematic.
Asks again what the reason is for prohibiting covering in an uncertain case.
Suggests the reason: he might crush the earth, which is forbidden labor on a Festival.
If crushing is the worry, the definite case should also be decreed prohibited, since crushing happens there too.
The positive mitzva of covering blood overrides the Festival prohibition on crushing, so definite cases are permitted.
Challenge from cases where a mitzva overrides a prohibition, such as circumcising a leprous foreskin or fringes on linen.
Distinguishes those cases: there one act fulfills the mitzva and uproots the prohibition, and here the crushing can be that same act.
Challenge: a Festival combines a positive rest commandment and a prohibition, and a positive mitzva alone does not override both.
Rava holds that the item must be intended for a definite mitzva beforehand; it cannot serve an unplanned purpose on a Festival.
Rava is consistent: earth brought for excrement may cover bird blood, but earth brought for bird blood may not cover excrement.
The Sages of Neharbela hold that even earth brought for bird blood may be used for excrement, since intent is not restricted.
Western scholars dispute whether a koy is like excrement; one position says it is, the other says it is not.
Concludes that Rava holds a koy is like excrement, supported by his earth ruling.
Rami bar Yeiva gives another reason: a rabbinic decree, lest people wrongly think a koy's forbidden fat is permitted.
If so, the koy's blood should also be prohibited on a weekday, for the same concern.
On a weekday people will think he is cleaning his courtyard, not performing the mitzva, so the concern does not arise.
Asks what can be said if he slaughtered in a dunghill, or came to consult a Sage on a weekday.
On a weekday Sages tell him to cover even when uncertain; on a Festival they would not, since that signals a koy is definitely undomesticated.
Rabbi Zeira's baraita: mixed blood of domesticated and undomesticated animals or fowl may not be covered on a Festival.
Rabbi Yosei bar Yasinia limits this: if the whole mixture can be covered with one thrust, covering it is permitted.
Asks why this is taught, since it seems obvious, and whether one thrust should be decreed prohibited.
The ruling is needed so one thrust is not decreed prohibited out of concern for two thrusts.
Rabba's ruling: if one slaughtered a bird on the eve of a Festival, its blood may not be covered on the Festival.

9a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If dough was kneaded on the Festival eve, its ḥalla may be separated on the Festival, since bread may not be eaten without it.
Shmuel's father rules that ḥalla may not be separated on the Festival if the dough could have been separated before it.
Challenge: Shmuel's ruling on ḥalla outside Eretz Yisrael implies separation is not required, contradicting Shmuel's father.
Rava replies that Shmuel himself admits ḥalla has sanctity, so he may agree with his father after all.
Mishna: Beit Shammai forbid moving a dovecote ladder between dovecotes, while Beit Hillel permit it.
Rav Ḥanan bar Ami explains the dispute applies only in the public domain, where onlookers might suspect forbidden labor.
Asks whether this is so, citing Rav's principle that even private acts forbidden due to appearances remain prohibited.
Replies that this is a dispute between tanna'im.
A baraita on drying wet clothes in the sun shows Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon forbid it even in private.
Another version: the dispute concerns the private domain, with Beit Shammai following Rav and Beit Hillel rejecting him.
Challenge: should Rav's view be read as following Beit Shammai, who alone hold that such acts are forbidden in private?
Rejects this: it is again a dispute between tanna'im.
The baraita with the same clothes case supports the tanna'im reading, and Rav follows Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon.

9b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna does not follow this tanna, as the Gemara introduces a baraita to show a different tanna's view.
Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: both schools permit carrying a ladder between dovecotes and disagree only about returning it.
Rabbi Yehuda limits the dispute to a dovecote ladder; an attic ladder is forbidden according to everyone.
Rabbi Dosa permits tilting a ladder between windows of one dovecote, and others add he may even shuffle it along.
Anecdote: Rabbi Hiyya's sons permitted moving an attic ladder, and their father told them to reverse the ruling.
Explains the sons' error: they inferred from Rabbi Yehuda that the first tanna holds the schools dispute attic ladders, which is not so.
Asks from where this inference about the first tanna can be drawn.
The mishna's wording of moving a ladder from dovecote to dovecote shows it refers only to dovecote ladders.
Asks what reasoning the sons had for their ruling.
The sons would reply that the baraita's phrase from one dovecote to another permits even moving between several dovecotes.
A different version: the sons were asked about tilting an attic ladder before the Festival and permitted it.
Explains the sons' reasoning as a reversal: they took Rabbi Dosa as more lenient, but he is actually stricter.
The mishna permits tilting a dovecote ladder, which the Gemara reads as Beit Shammai being stringent and Beit Hillel lenient on Festival joy.
Contradiction from the slaughter ruling: Beit Shammai allow covering blood with a shovel, while Beit Hillel forbid slaughter without prepared earth.
Rabbi Yoḥanan answers that the schools' opinions are reversed in attribution.
Challenge: why infer full reversal? Beit Shammai may permit covering only where a shovel is already embedded in the earth.
Alternative: Beit Hillel permit only where the dovecote itself shows the ladder's purpose, so no real contradiction remains.
Retracting, the Gemara brings a mishna on taking fledglings on a Festival, where the schools' stances on preparation also differ.
Restating: on Festival joy, Beit Shammai are stringent and Beit Hillel lenient, so the contradiction returns.
The contradiction is raised again from the slaughter ruling, which Rabbi Yoḥanan's reversal was meant to resolve.
Challenge to Rabbi Yoḥanan: perhaps Beit Shammai permit covering only where an embedded shovel is present.

10a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the earlier resolution: without an embedded shovel even Beit Shammai forbid, and Beit Hillel's leniency applies only to muktze items.
Mishna: Beit Shammai forbid cutting meat with a large pestle on a Festival, while Beit Hillel permit it.
Inference from the pestle ruling: Beit Shammai are stringent and Beit Hillel lenient regarding Festival joy.
Contradiction with the slaughter ruling, which leads Rabbi Yoḥanan to reverse the attribution of the opinions.
Rejects Rabbi Yoḥanan: perhaps Beit Shammai permit covering only where a shovel is embedded and prepared.
Alternative: Beit Hillel are lenient only where the item has the status of a vessel, not in the slaughter case.
Mishna: Beit Shammai forbid placing or lifting an untanned hide on a Festival, while Beit Hillel permit placing it.
Restating the inference that Beit Shammai are stringent and Beit Hillel lenient on Festival joy, with the same contradiction.
The same contradiction is raised, and Rabbi Yoḥanan again says the attribution of the opinions is reversed.
Rejects this again: Beit Shammai may permit covering only where a shovel is embedded, not otherwise.
Alternative: Beit Hillel are lenient only for a hide suited to reclining, which is not fully muktze, unlike slaughter.
Mishna: Beit Shammai forbid removing store shutters on a Festival, while Beit Hillel permit even replacing them.
Inference that Beit Shammai are stringent and Beit Hillel lenient on Festival joy, so the slaughter contradiction arises again.
Raises the slaughter contradiction once more, now involving Beit Shammai against Beit Hillel on covering blood.
Resolves the contradictions: Beit Shammai's two rulings differ by an embedded shovel, and Beit Hillel's by no Torah prohibition on vessels.
Mishna: Beit Shammai forbid taking fledgling doves unless shaken while it is still day, while Beit Hillel only require standing and declaring.
Rav Ḥanan bar Ami explains the dispute concerns the first brood, where Beit Shammai decree lest one change his mind.
Asks why Beit Hillel require declaring this one and that one, rather than naming the dovecote from which he will take them.
Hypothesis: perhaps Beit Hillel do not accept retroactive designation of intention.
Mishna in Ohalot on a corpse in a house with many entrances, where intent to remove it through one entrance affects impurity.
Beit Shammai require the intention to exist before death, while Beit Hillel accept retroactive designation.
Refutes the proof: Rabba and Rav Oshaya say Beit Hillel purify only from that point forward, rejecting retroactive designation.
Rava's resolution: Beit Hillel accept retroactive designation for impurity, but fledglings are restricted to avoid moving muktze.
Objection: if standing and declaring suffices, the concern about changing one's mind and handling them should not arise.
Replies: the declaration works only when made on the eve of the Festival, since one then cannot alter the choice on the day.

10b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the prior ruling: fat and thin birds may be mistaken, and announcing the choice a day earlier prevents this.
Mishna: fledglings designated for slaughter on the Festival eve are forbidden if others are found, but permitted if only designated ones remain.
Asks why it is obvious that fledglings found in a different color are not the designated ones.
Rabba explains the case: both colors were designated and swapped places, and the designated ones are presumed to have left.
Suggests the mishna supports Rabbi Ḥanina's principle that the majority rule overrides the proximate source.
Restates the mishna: if two were designated and three found, the fledglings are forbidden.
Explains either way the fledglings are forbidden: the others are unmarked, or one unmarked bird is mixed in.
Restates the mishna: if three were designated and two found, the fledglings are permitted.
Explains that these are the same birds and one has flown off, leaving two behind.
Suggests the mishna follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, citing a baraita on tithe money and its converse case.
The Gemara refutes this: Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Elazar say fledglings differ because they hop away, unlike pouches.
Asks why this answer is needed, since Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Elazar dispute the pouch case itself.
Shows that the answer about fledglings is needed only on one view of the pouch dispute, and not on the other.
Rav Ashi: the case is tied fledglings and tied pouches, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi replies that pouches too may come apart.

11a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains that a worn knot may come undone, so it is possible someone took only one of the two pouches.
Mishna: fledglings designated inside the nest but found before it are forbidden.
Suggests the mishna supports Rabbi Ḥanina's principle that the majority rule applies when the item is nearby.
Abaye refutes this with a ledge, and Rava limits the case to adjacent nests, where fledglings may have descended from either.
Alternative case: fledglings in the upper or lower nest may have come from the other, so the mishna's permitted case requires no other birds.
Asks what the actual circumstances of the mishna are, if the fledglings can already fly away.
Mar Ukva bar Ḥama holds that a hopping creature never hops more than fifty cubits, so the nest distance matters.
Explains that the other nest must be around a corner, since a fledgling keeps hopping while it can see its nest.
Mishna: Beit Shammai forbid moving a pestle and a hide on a Festival, while Beit Hillel permit both.
Baraita: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that a pestle used to cut meat may not be moved further on the Festival.
Abaye holds the dispute concerns only a pestle, while a wooden anvil for breaking bones is permitted by all.
Asks why this needs saying, since the mishna mentions only a pestle.
Abaye's teaching is needed lest one think the dispute extends to a wooden anvil, showing Beit Hillel's far-reaching leniency.
Alternative version: even a new wooden anvil is permitted, lest one reconsider and set it aside for another use.
Asks whether Beit Shammai are not concerned that one might reconsider, citing their ruling on animals and knives.
Tosefta: Beit Shammai forbid bringing a butcher and knife near an animal, or spices and a pestle near a mortar, out of concern for reconsidering.
Refutes the comparison: an animal or pot may be set aside on reconsideration, but a slaughtered animal's bones must be broken.
Mishna restated: Beit Shammai forbid placing an unprocessed hide before those who will tread on it, a tanning labor.
Tosefta: both schools agree one may salt meat for roasting on the hide, since salt is not expected to fall on it.
Abaye limits this to meat salted for roasting; meat salted for cooking in a pot may not be salted on the hide.
Asks whether salting for cooking is obviously forbidden, since the Tosefta specifies only roasting.
Baraita: fats may not be salted or turned on the Festival, but Rabbi Yehoshua permits spreading them in the wind on pegs.
Rav Mattana rules on the halakha in Rabbi Yehoshua's dispute, with a variant attribution of the ruling.
Explains why the ruling is needed: lest one think majority rules, or that Rabbi Yehoshua's reasoning should prevail to avoid refusal to slaughter.
Asks how this differs from the hide case, where Beit Hillel permit placing it because otherwise one would refrain from slaughter.

11b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains that spreading a hide is not clearly for tanning, unlike fats, where the permitted reason could lead to salting hides.
Shmuel permits salting several pieces at once on a Festival, and the mishna records Beit Shammai forbidding and Beit Hillel permitting shutter removal and replacement.
Asks what the shutters are; Ulla explains they are shop shutters, opened so people can settle accounts with storekeepers.
Ulla lists three cases where a permitted action with undesirable result encourages a desirable one, and Rahava adds a case of a ḥaver's barrel.
Asks why Ulla restates a mishna teaching about spreading out a hide.
Lest one think Beit Hillel's reason is the hide's fitness for reclining, so the leniency is a general principle that applies only on the Festival.
Asks why Ulla restates the mishna on replacing shop shutters, which the Gemara already learned.
Lest one think Beit Hillel's reason is that vessels may be dismantled, Ulla clarifies the leniency applies to shops, not houses.
Asks why Ulla restates the Temple bandage ruling, already learned in the mishna.
Lest one think the rabbinic labor prohibition is lifted throughout the Temple, the leniency applies only to priests who serve.
Asks what is added by listing Rahava's barrel case, given that the tanna'im dispute whether one may finish selling.
Lest one think finishing sales is allowed because impurity does not apply on a Festival, the leniency applies only if the sale began.
Asks why Ulla omitted this case from his list of examples.
Ulla listed only unanimous cases, since Beit Shammai's opinion is disregarded when opposed to Beit Hillel.
Introduces Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's view that the mishna is not in accordance with this tanna.
Baraita: both schools agree shutters may be removed, and disagree only on replacing them, with a permitted case when there is no hinge.
Challenge: another baraita says the schools disagree only when there is no hinge, and all agree it is forbidden if there is one.
Abaye reconciles the baraitot: a hinge on the side is forbidden by all, no hinge is permitted, and the dispute concerns a hinge in the middle.

12a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: One Sage forbids a middle hinge because of a side hinge, while another does not issue that decree, since such a hinge is not building.
Mishna: Beit Shammai forbid carrying a minor, a lulav, or a Torah scroll into the public domain on a Festival, while Beit Hillel permit it.
Baraita: one who slaughters a gift offering on a Festival is flogged, since the slaughter was not for eating.
Rav Yitzḥak bar Avdimi objects that the baraita follows Beit Shammai, and that Beit Hillel would permit slaughter for any beneficial purpose.
Rabba objects that the schools may instead dispute eiruv and carrying out on a Festival, which the baraita does not establish.
Explains Rabba's reading: Beit Shammai hold eiruv and carrying out apply on a Festival, while Beit Hillel derive from Jeremiah that they do not.
Rav Yosef objects: then muktze would also be permitted, so the dispute must concern carrying out only for a non-food purpose.
Rabbi Yoḥanan also holds the schools dispute whether a carrying permitted for food is permitted for other purposes.
Baraita on cooking the sciatic nerve in milk on a Festival: the offender is flogged for five separate prohibitions.

12b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The ruling rests on the reason that kindling a fire is prohibited on a Festival.
Rabbi Yochanan dismisses the baraita as unfit for study and not a mishna worthy of acceptance.
Beit Shammai's reasoning: permissions for carrying and kindling for food do not extend to other purposes.
The Gemara explains that this baraita cannot follow Beit Hillel, who would extend such permissions to non-food purposes.
The Mishna: separating challah is allowed on a Festival, and the schools disagree about bringing gifts to priests.
Beit Shammai argue by analogy from teruma: since it cannot be brought on a Festival, neither can other gifts.
Beit Hillel reply that the analogy fails, since separating the other gifts is permitted on a Festival.
The Gemara proposes reading the Mishna as referring to animals slaughtered on the Festival or the evening before.
The Gemara asks whose opinion the Mishna then represents.
It cannot be Rabbi Yosei or Rabbi Yehuda; it must be the view of the Aherim.
A Tosefta is quoted, attributing to Rabbi Yehuda an account of the dispute about gifts separated before the Festival.
Beit Shammai reason by analogy from teruma to the other gifts in this version of the dispute.
Beit Hillel reply that the analogy fails, since separation of the other gifts is permitted on the Festival.
Rabbi Yosei disputes this record: the disagreement concerned only teruma, not the other gifts.
Beit Hillel argue by analogy that since the other gifts may be brought, teruma may be brought too.
Beit Shammai reply that the analogy fails, since separating teruma is itself forbidden on the Festival.
The Aherim say the dispute concerned only the other gifts, not teruma.
The Gemara proposes the Mishna follows the Aherim rather than Rabbi Yehuda, and challenges that identification.
Rava reads the Mishna as concerning animals slaughtered the evening before and separated on the Festival.
Why not say the Mishna follows Rabbi Yehuda rather than the Aherim, given this reading?
Even if the Mishna follows the Aherim, they disputed only about animals slaughtered the evening before.
If so, the Aherim and Rabbi Yehuda agree, so what is the practical difference between their views?
Rav Yehuda said in Shmuel's name that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei.
Rav Tovi asks Rav Yosef whether teruma wine may be brought to a priest on the Festival.
Rav Yosef replies by citing Rav Yehuda's report of Shmuel: the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei.
Rava's host asks whether crushing mustard stalks and eating from them is permitted on a Festival, and brings the question to Rava.
Rava cites a baraita permitting one to husk kernels and crush legumes on a Festival.
Abaye objects with a baraita restricting winnowing and sifting on the Festival eve, challenging Rava's reading.
The Gemara answers that the baraita's latter clause mirrors its Shabbat clause, so no prohibition is implied on the Festival itself.
Abaye presses a second objection: if crushing is permitted, teruma could be separated on the Festival, contradicting the Mishna.
The Gemara answers that this difficulty is not a real problem.

13a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita presents Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Yehuda as disagreeing about teruma from grain still on the stalk.
The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Yehuda: a case exists where he too must separate teruma from unprocessed grain.
Rather, the teruma both schools agree may not be separated on a Festival is the usual kind, from threshed grain.
Abaye limits the dispute to grain stalks; for legumes, everyone agrees the bundles are already subject to teruma.
The Gemara offers a Mishna about fenugreek bundles as support for Abaye's reading.
The Gemara rejects the proof: the fenugreek Mishna may follow Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who obligates teruma on stalks.
Why then single out fenugreek? If the Mishna follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, grain stalks are included anyway; if Rabbi Yosei, other legumes should be listed.
Fenugreek is mentioned to exclude the idea that its stalks, sharing the same flavor as its fruit, also require teruma.
Some attribute to Abaye the view that the dispute concerns only grain stalks, while legumes are not yet tithable.
An objection from the fenugreek Mishna: its ruling may refer to ordinary untithed produce, contrary to Abaye's reading.
The Gemara rejects the objection: the case concerns first tithe, which remains untithed until its teruma is separated.
Rabbi Abbahu cites Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish on the correct order: teruma from the grain first, and only then first tithe.
If first tithe was separated while the grain was still on the stalks, it is treated as untithed for the teruma of the tithe.
If naming makes first tithe untithed, why must it be pounded? The Levite could simply return the grain in its current state.
Rava explains that this is a penalty: the Levite took his tithe prematurely, so he must improve the produce before separating.
A baraita is cited in support: a Levite given stalks must process them, and only then separate teruma of the tithe.

13b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara concludes that teruma of the tithe, like teruma gedola, is separated only from the granary and winepress.
If first tithe is meant, why does the Mishna say calculates rather than measures, since the tithe requires exact measure?
The Mishna follows Abba Elazar ben Gimmel, who derives from a verse that teruma of the tithe, like teruma gedola, may be set aside by estimate and intention.
Rabbi Abbahu cites Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish: first tithe separated while the grain is on the stalks stays untithed until its teruma of the tithe is set aside.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind that ruling.
Rava explains: once the first tithe has acquired its name, the obligation of teruma of the tithe takes effect as well.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish adds that first tithe separated from unthreshed grain is exempt from teruma gedola.
A verse is cited: teruma of the tithe is taken from the tithe itself, so the Levite owes no teruma gedola from that first tithe.
Rav Pappa challenges Abaye: if so, first tithe separated even after the grain was piled should also be exempt from teruma gedola.
Abaye replies with a verse requiring teruma gedola from all produce, including the tithe, so the exemption cannot extend to piled grain.
The Gemara asks what distinguishes grain on the stalk from threshed piled grain in this respect.
The Gemara cites the Mishna on peeling barley and Rabbi Elazar's extension of its rule to Shabbat.
The Gemara asks: did Rav's wife not peel barley on Shabbat by the cupful? It suggests Rabbi Elazar's comment applies to a different clause.
Rabbi Abba bar Memel objects: if completing labor for tithes counts as completing it, the same should hold for Shabbat, which is far stricter.
Rav Sheshet objects: tithes are sometimes stricter than Shabbat, so the claimed inconsistency is no difficulty.
Mishnayot on the granary for tithes are cited: vegetables become tithable when piled, though piling on Shabbat is not forbidden labor.
Shabbat prohibits only planned creative labor, which piling is not; the barley case follows the same reasoning.
The Gemara asks how one may husk grain on a Festival.
Rav Yosef's transmitted rulings allow rubbing between fingers; Rava adds that altering the manner of the act permits even more.
The Gemara asks how one may blow on grain to winnow it in a permitted way on Shabbat.
Rav Adda bar Ahava cites Rav on how one may blow in a permitted manner, and the explanation continues beyond this daf.

14a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara describes the manner of blowing: the grain is held on the fingers rather than in the palm, an unusual method.
The Gemara reports that Eretz Yisrael scholars mocked this explanation, arguing that any altered manner should permit using the whole hand.
Rav Elazar's halakha: one may blow holding grain in one hand, not two, and with full strength, since it is not like prohibited labor.
Beit Shammai: spices may be pounded in a slightly unusual way with a wooden pestle, and salt only with a flask or a wooden ladle.
Beit Hillel: spices may be pounded in the usual way, even with a stone pestle, while salt needs only a slight modification such as a wooden pestle.
Everyone agrees that pounding salt on a Festival requires an irregular manner.
Rav Huna's reason: everyone knows all dishes need salt, so it should have been prepared in advance, while not all dishes need spices.
Rav Hisda's reason: spices lose their flavor and cannot be prepared ahead, while salt keeps, so it should have been prepared earlier.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two reasons, and answers with the cases of known dishes and saffron.
Shmuel's ruling: all foods that must be pounded may be pounded in the usual manner, even salt.
The Gemara challenges: didn't you say that salt requires an irregular manner in everyone's view?
Shmuel stated his ruling following the one tanna who holds that salt may be pounded in the usual way.
A baraita of Rabbi Meir: the schools disagree only about pounding salt alone; Beit Shammai restrict it, while Beit Hillel permit it in any manner.
The Gemara is surprised that Beit Hillel would allow any manner, and revises the wording to say the permission applies to any purpose.
Rav Aha Bardela instructs his son to tilt the pestle slightly, so that salt is pounded in a somewhat different manner on a Festival.
Rav Sheshet hears pounding on a Festival and concludes the sound cannot come from his household, which he instructed not to do so.
The Gemara asks: perhaps they tilted the pestle in a permitted manner?
No: Rav Sheshet heard a clear sound, unlike the sound of a tilted pestle.
The Gemara asks: perhaps they were pounding spices, which may be pounded in the usual way on a Festival?
The sound of pounded spices is distinctive, like a bark, and Rav Sheshet would have recognized it.
A baraita teaches that on a Festival one may not prepare groats or grind grain with a mortar and pestle.
The Gemara explains the baraita as amended: groats are forbidden because grinding in a mortar is forbidden.
Stating only the mortar rule would suggest a small mortar is permitted, so the tanna adds that groats are forbidden in every manner.
The Gemara challenges the reading: another baraita explicitly permits grinding in a small mortar, which seems to conflict with the ban on groats.
Abaye replies that the first baraita also refers only to a large mortar, so the baraita states two separate rulings.

14b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava resolves the apparent contradiction: the small-mortar ruling applies to Babylonians, who lack servants, while the stricter ruling applies in Eretz Yisrael.
The story of Rav Pappi, who declined to eat porridge at Mar Shmuel's house on a Festival, fearing the grain was pounded that day.
The Gemara asks: perhaps they pounded it in a small mortar, which is permitted?
Rav Pappi saw the grain was finely ground, which a small mortar cannot achieve.
The Gemara asks: perhaps they prepared it the day before the Festival?
The husks were bright, showing recent preparation; alternatively, Mar Shmuel's household had lax servants, so he should have banned all grinding.
The Mishna: Beit Shammai allow one to select legumes and eat the selected food immediately, leaving the refuse.
Beit Hillel allow selecting in the usual way, in one's lap or with a tray or large vessel, but not with tools designed for selecting.
Rabban Gamliel adds that one may wash legumes in water and skim off the floating refuse.
A baraita explains Rabban Gamliel: usual selecting is permitted when the food outweighs the refuse; if the refuse outweighs it, one must take the food.
The Gemara asks whether any opinion permits usual selection when the refuse outweighs the food.
No: the case is refuse that takes more effort to remove yet is smaller in quantity, so one should take the food.
Rabban Gamliel restates his view that one may wash legumes in water and skim off the refuse.
A Tosefta describes the custom of Rabban Gamliel's house: lentils in a bucket of water, so the food sinks and the refuse floats up.
The Gemara asks: isn't the opposite taught in another baraita, where the food rises and the refuse sinks?
The baraitot differ by type of refuse: earth sinks below lentils, while straw floats on water.
The Mishna: Beit Shammai permit sending only prepared food on a Festival, not other gifts.
Beit Hillel permit sending domesticated and wild animals and fowl, living or slaughtered, plus wines, oils, flour and legumes, but not grain.
Rabbi Shimon permits sending grain as well, since it can be made into porridge without grinding.
Rav Yehiel teaches that sending is permitted provided it is not done in a convoy that looks like transporting merchandise.
A baraita defines a convoy as at least three people, so fewer than three is permitted.
Rav Ashi asks: is three people carrying three kinds of food a convoy, or is each item separate? The question is left unresolved.
The Gemara notes the Mishna's ruling that Rabbi Shimon permits sending grain.
A baraita illustrates Rabbi Shimon's view: wheat for ludiyot cookies, barley for animal feed, and lentils for crushed resisin.
The Mishna: one may send clothes, sewn or unsewn, even of mixed wool and linen, if they serve the Festival; but not a spiked sandal or unsewn shoe.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that a white shoe may not be sent, since it needs an artisan to blacken it; anything usable on the Festival may be sent.
The Gemara asks: sewn and unsewn clothes have uses, but for what use is a mixed-fiber garment suited, if it cannot be worn?
Proposed answer: a mixed-fiber garment may be spread beneath oneself.
A baraita cites Leviticus 19:19 and holds that the Sages prohibited even spreading a mixed garment beneath oneself, lest a thread wind around the flesh.
Proposed refinement: the allowance applies when something separates the mixed garment from the body.
The Gemara objects with a tradition that even ten mattresses over a mixed cloth may not be slept on, per Leviticus 19:19.
Rather, the Mishna refers to a mixed-fiber curtain, which is not an item of clothing.
The Gemara objects: Ulla taught that curtains are impure because attendants warm themselves with them, so a mixed-fiber curtain used like a blanket should be forbidden too.

15a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rather, the ruling concerns hard clothing: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua holds that hard felt from Neresh may be sat on despite its mixed fibers.
Rav Pappa: felt socks are hard, so the prohibition of mixed fibers does not apply to them.
Rava: hard coin bundles are permitted, but seed pouches, which are larger and softer, are prohibited as mixed fibers.
Rav Ashi: both are permitted, since using them is not the usual way of keeping warm, even against the skin.
The Mishna prohibits sending a spiked sandal on a Festival.
The Gemara asks: what is the reason spiked sandals may not be worn?
It is due to an incident in which people wearing spiked sandals on Shabbat caused a great tragedy, which prompted a decree.
Abaye: a spiked sandal may not be worn on Shabbat, but it may be moved.
Abaye infers from the Mishna's wording: if moving were prohibited, stating that sending is forbidden would be superfluous.
The Gemara asks: isn't it obvious that an unsewn shoe may not be sent, since it is unfit for wearing?
The Mishna is needed for a shoe fastened with pins, which can be worn yet is still not sent.
The Mishna cites Rabbi Yehuda: even a white shoe may not be sent.
A baraita: Rabbi Yehuda permits black but forbids white shoes, while Rabbi Yosei forbids black ones because they require polishing.
The Gemara explains there is no real dispute: each Sage ruled according to the leather custom of his locale.
The general principle: any article usable on a Festival may be sent on a Festival.
Rav Sheshet permitted the Sages to send phylacteries on a Festival.
Abaye objects: the general principle excludes phylacteries, which are not worn on Festivals.
The Mishna means: anything usable on a weekday may be sent on a Festival.
Abaye's novel ruling: a traveler with phylacteries on his head when the day becomes holy covers them with his hand until he reaches home.
Rav Huna bar Rav Ika objects with a baraita: phylacteries are carried only to the nearest safe house inside the city, not all the way home.
The baraitot differ by safeguarding: where phylacteries can be guarded at the nearest house, one leaves them there; otherwise one brings them home.
Why specify phylacteries on one's head? A pair found on the ground should also be donned and carried in, per the Eiruvin mishna.
The baraitot differ by protection: one case is guarded from both thieves and dogs, while the mishna case is guarded only from dogs.
Lest one think most thieves are Jews who would not disdain phylacteries, the Mishna teaches that the minority case is still taken into account.
Chapter-closing formula marking the end of the chapter of Beitzah.

15b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: on a Festival eve preceding Shabbat, one may cook for the Festival and rely on a prepared dish for Shabbat.
Beit Shammai require two cooked dishes for the joining of cooked foods.
Beit Hillel require one dish; both schools agree that a fish with an egg fried on it counts as two dishes.
If the eiruv was eaten or lost, one may not initially cook for Shabbat; if some remains, one may rely on it.
The Gemara asks: what is the source of the eiruv tavshilin halakha?
Shmuel derives it from the verse to remember Shabbat, which teaches guarding Shabbat from being forgotten on another day.
The Gemara asks: what is the reason for this ordinance?
Rava: the Sages ensured one selects a choice portion for Shabbat and a separate one for the Festival.
Rav Ashi: the ordinance prevents people concluding that one may bake on a Festival for Shabbat, a fortiori for a weekday.
The Gemara cites the Mishna: one prepares a dish on Festival eve and relies on it for Shabbat.
For Rav Ashi it makes sense: baking for Shabbat is permitted on the eve, but not on the Festival itself.
But for Rava, why does the Mishna specify the eve at all?
Even on the Festival itself the goal could be achieved; yes, indeed.
Rather, it is a decree lest one be negligent and fail to prepare the eiruv at all.
A verse, Exodus 16:23, is cited: bake and cook what you will, and set aside the rest for Shabbat.
From this verse Rabbi Eliezer derives that baking for Shabbat on a Festival requires an existing baked item; the Sages based the eiruv on it.
A baraita tells of Rabbi Eliezer lecturing on Festival halakhot while groups of students left, each named for a kind of vessel.
When a sixth group left, Rabbi Eliezer cursed them, and the remaining students turned pale, fearing he meant them.
Rabbi Eliezer tells his students he meant the departed, who abandon eternal life for temporary pleasures.
He quotes Nehemiah 8:10: eat fat, drink sweet, send portions, for the joy of the Lord is your strength.
The Master says the departing students left eternal life for temporary life.
The Gemara asks: isn't the joy of the Festival itself a mitzva, and so part of eternal life?
Rabbi Eliezer follows his view that Festival joy is optional, not a mitzva.
A baraita: Rabbi Eliezer holds that on a Festival a person may only eat and drink, or sit and study.
Rabbi Yehoshua says: divide the day, half for God and half for yourselves.
Rabbi Yoḥanan says both sages derived their views from one verse.
Two verses are cited: one says the assembly is for the Lord, the other says it is for you.
The Gemara asks: how are these two views reconciled?
Rabbi Eliezer: the day is entirely for God or entirely for you; Rabbi Yehoshua: split it between both.
The Gemara asks what 'for whom nothing is prepared' means.
Rav Ḥisda: it refers to one who could not prepare an eiruv and must rely on others for Shabbat food.
Others say: aid is owed only to one who had no chance to prepare an eiruv; one who could but did not is negligent.
The Gemara asks what the verse 'the joy of the Lord is your strength' means.
Rabbi Yoḥanan cites God's words: borrow for My sake, sanctify Shabbat and Festivals with wine, and trust Me to repay.
Rabbi Yoḥanan cites Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon: one who wants his property preserved should plant an eder tree among it.
Psalm 93:4 is cited: the Lord on high is mighty, adir, which the Gemara links to eder.
Alternatively, the eder's name itself suggests endurance for many generations.
A baraita: a field containing an eder tree cannot be stolen or seized, and its fruit is preserved.
Rav Taḥlifa, brother of Ravnai Ḥoza'a, begins a further teaching that continues beyond this daf.

16a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A person's livelihood is fixed from Rosh HaShana to Yom Kippur, except for expenses on Shabbat, Festivals, and sons' Torah schooling, which are adjusted.
Rabbi Abbahu asks which verse supports this dictum.
Psalm 81 is cited: the concealed new moon is Rosh HaShana, and the verse calls the day a statute for Israel.
The Gemara asks how we know that the word statute (ḥok) refers to food.
Genesis 47:22 uses ḥok for allotted food, and Mar Zutra adds Proverbs 30:8 about my allotted bread.
A baraita: Shammai the Elder always ate choice food to honor Shabbat, setting aside the better animal for Shabbat.
Hillel's distinct trait: all his actions, even on weekdays, were for the sake of Heaven.
Psalm 68:20 is cited: Blessed be the Lord day by day, showing God blesses each day.
Beit Shammai: from the first day of the week one begins preparing for Shabbat.
Beit Hillel cite the verse day by day as their basis, a view that differs from Beit Shammai's advance preparation.
Rabbi Ḥama bar Ḥanina: one giving a gift need not inform the recipient, citing Moses, who did not know his face shone.
The Gemara objects: God told Moses to announce Shabbat as a gift, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel requires informing the mother of a gift.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: one who gives bread to a child must inform the child's mother.
The cases differ: a gift likely to be revealed, like Moses' shining face, needs no announcement; Shabbat's reward is not likely to be revealed.
The Master's earlier statement: one who gives bread to a child must inform his mother.
The Gemara asks: how does one inform the child's mother?
He rubs oil on the child and paints his eyes with kohl, so the mother asks who did it.
The Gemara asks: what should be done nowadays, when such painting may be seen as sorcery?
Rav Pappa: rub the child with the same kind of food placed on the bread, such as butter or cheese.
Rabbi Yoḥanan cites Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai: all mitzvot were given publicly except Shabbat, which was given privately.
Exodus 31:17 is cited: it is a sign between Me and the children of Israel forever, a matter kept private.
The Gemara objects: if Shabbat was given privately, gentiles should not be punished for rejecting it.
God informed them of Shabbat's concept but not its reward; alternatively, they were told the reward but not the extra soul.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish: God gives each person an extra soul on Shabbat eve and removes it at its end.
Exodus 31:17 vayinafash is expounded: woe for the lost extra soul, nefesh.
The Mishna's ruling: one may prepare a cooked dish on Festival eve and rely on it for Shabbat.
Abaye: the eiruv works only with a cooked dish, not with bread alone.
The Gemara asks why bread is unfit: if an accompaniment is needed, porridge fails too, as Rabbi Zeira's Babylonians ate bread with bread.
Rav Neḥumi bar Zekharya: one may establish an eiruv with porridge, since the requirement is a non-routine item.
A variant version: Abaye held that bread alone does not suffice for the eiruv.
The Gemara asks the reason: porridge is not routine, so why is it not accepted if a non-routine item is required?
Rav Neḥumi in Abaye's name: one needs an accompaniment to bread; porridge is not one, as Rabbi Zeira's citation shows.
Rabbi Ḥiyya: lentils left at the bottom of a pot may be relied on for an eiruv, if there is an olive-bulk of them.
Rav Yitzḥak bar Rav Yehuda: fat on a knife may be scraped off and used for an eiruv, if an olive-bulk is present.
Rav Asi citing Rav: small salted fish cooked by a gentile are not considered a gentile's cooked food.
Rav Yosef: even if a gentile roasted such fish, a Jew may rely on them for an eiruv.
If a gentile made them into fish fried in oil and flour, they are prohibited, since his cooking made them noteworthy food.
The Gemara challenges: this is obvious and need not be taught.

16b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Clarifies that the flour, not the fish fat, is the essential ingredient that makes the dish prohibited.
Rabbi Abba states that a joining of cooked foods requires an olive-bulk of food.
Asks whether one olive-bulk suffices for the whole household or each person needs a separate one.
Rav's ruling is cited as support: one olive-bulk is required whether for one person or for a hundred.
A mishnah is cited: if the eiruv was eaten or lost, one may rely on any remaining portion.
Asks what the mishnah means by any amount whatsoever.
Rejects the literal reading: the remainder must still be at least an olive-bulk.
A baraita lists acceptable cooked dishes and says the eiruv has no measure at its start or end.
Asks whether having no measure means no minimum at all, not even an olive-bulk.
No: there is no maximum size, but a minimum of an olive-bulk does apply.
Rav Huna, citing Rav, teaches that a joining of cooked foods requires the preparer's awareness.
The Gemara explains that the preparer's awareness is obviously required.
Asks whether the awareness of the person the eiruv is for is also needed.
Testimonies that Shmuel's father and Rabbis Ami and Asi prepared eiruvin for entire cities support the answer.
Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi announced that anyone without an eiruv could rely on his.
Asks how far away one may live and still rely on such an eiruv.
Rav Nachumi, citing Abaye, says one may rely on it up to the Shabbat limit.
Narrative: a blind man reciting mishnayot before Shmuel appeared sad.
Shmuel asks the man why he is sad.
The man explains that he did not prepare an eiruv before the Festival.
Shmuel tells him to rely on his own eiruv for the year.
The next year Shmuel again notices the man looking sad.
Shmuel asks again why he is sad.
The man repeats that he did not prepare an eiruv.
Shmuel rules that the man is negligent, so others may rely on his eiruv but he may not.
A baraita: when a Festival falls on Shabbat eve, neither type of eiruv may be prepared.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi permits preparing an eiruv of courtyards on that Festival.
Explains Rabbi's distinction: one may forbid what is forbidden to a person, not what is permitted to him.
Rav holds the halakha follows the first tanna, while Shmuel holds it follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
Asks whether ruling like Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi is a leniency or a stringency.
Obviously it is a leniency, because the ruling was stated as such.
Rabbi Elazar sent word that the Babylonian version reverses the opinions of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the Sages.
Asks what the conclusive ruling is.
Rav Tachlifa bar Avdimi acted on Shmuel's ruling, offered as proof of the lenient reading.
Rav reacted angrily: the first public ruling of this young scholar corrupts the halakha.
If Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi meant leniency, the corruption makes sense; if stringency, what corruption is there?
The ruling corrupts the behavior of the masses, who might then carry on Shabbat by mistake.

17a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains that this is the corruption the ruling would cause, so it cannot prove the conclusive halakha.
Rava, citing Rav Chisda and Rav Huna, rules that halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, prohibiting both types of eiruv.
A baraita opens the Festival-on-Shabbat prayer dispute, giving Beit Shammai's view of eight blessings with separate insertions.
Beit Hillel hold seven blessings, the middle one beginning and ending with Shabbat and mentioning the day's sanctity.
