Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi adds that the middle blessing concludes with Who sanctifies Shabbat, Israel and the seasons.
A tanna before Ravina gives a variant: the closing formula reads Who sanctifies Israel, Shabbat and the seasons.
Ravina objects: this implies Israel sanctifies Shabbat, yet Shabbat was already sanctified from creation.
Ravina proposes amended wording, so that Israel sanctifies the new moons and festivals while Shabbat is named first.
Rav Yosef rules that halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Ravina's resolution of the difficulty.
A baraita: when Shabbat falls on Rosh Chodesh or intermediate festival days, one recites the event passage in the Temple-service blessing, and if omitted, one repeats.
Rabbi Eliezer disagrees, placing the passage in the thanksgiving blessing, and in the additional prayer the middle blessing begins and ends with Shabbat.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, apply that Shabbat pattern to every seven-blessing prayer.
Rav Huna rules that halakha does not follow that pair, but the first tanna's view.
Rav Chiyya bar Ashi, citing Rav, permits placing an eiruv for boundaries on the first Festival day for the next, conditioned on doubt about which day is the Festival.
Rava permits placing an eiruv of cooked foods on the first Festival day for the next, with a conditional stipulation.
The Gemara explains that whoever permits the boundary eiruv a fortiori permits the cooked-food eiruv, but not the reverse.
Asks the reason for the difference between the two eiruvin.
A baraita forbids baking on one Festival day for the next, then introduces the established exceptions.
The established rule: a woman may fill a whole pot with meat and a baker a whole barrel with water, but may bake only what is needed that day.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar permits filling the whole oven with bread, because bread bakes better in a full oven.
Rava rules that halakha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.
Dilemma: if one did not prepare a cooked-food eiruv, is his flour also prohibited, or only his own labor?
Asks what practical difference the answer to this dilemma makes.
Explains the difference: if the flour is prohibited too, he must transfer it to others so they can bake for him.
Asks what the halakha is in the end.
Baraita: one who did not prepare a cooked-food eiruv may not bake, cook or insulate for himself or others, nor may others do so for him.
The baraita asks what such a person should do so that he has food for Shabbat.
He transfers his flour to others, who may then bake and cook for him.
Learns from this that he is prohibited and his flour is also prohibited.
Dilemma: if one baked on the Festival without a cooked-food eiruv, what is the halakha?
Brings a baraita as proof: he transfers his flour to others, and then others bake and cook for him.

17b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that if the bread were permitted, the baraita would have said so; it teaches only the permitted remedy.
Rav Adda bar Mattana replies that there is no proof, since the tanna taught only a permitted remedy and not a prohibited one.
A baraita: one who prepared an eiruv may bake, cook and insulate for Shabbat; if he ate it first, he and others may not do so for him.
The baraita continues: he may cook for the Festival and keep leftovers for Shabbat, unless he uses artifice, in which case the food is forbidden.
Rav Ashi replies that artifice differs, since the Sages were stricter with one who circumvents a prohibition than with a deliberate violator.
Rav Nachman says the baraita reflects Chananya's view, which aligns with Beit Shammai, so it is not a general proof.
Chananya's baraita, following Beit Shammai: baking requires an eiruv of bread, cooking requires a cooked dish, and insulating requires food insulated earlier.
Beit Hillel permit one cooked dish for all needs of baking, cooking and insulating.
A mishna: one who unwittingly tithed produce on Shabbat may eat it, but not if he did so intentionally.
Rejects the proof: the rule applies where he has other produce, so the Sages may have been lenient for one with no food.
A baraita: one who immerses vessels on Shabbat may use them if done unwittingly, but not if done intentionally.
Rejects the proof: the case concerns one who has other vessels or can borrow them, so the example is not forced.
Another baraita: one who cooks on Shabbat unwittingly may eat the food, but not if he cooked intentionally.
The Shabbat prohibition is different, since it carries karet and court execution, so the stringency does not transfer.
The mishna: Beit Shammai require two cooked dishes for a joining of cooked foods, while Beit Hillel require one.
Explains that the mishna does not follow this particular tanna's view.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar teaches that both schools agree that two dishes are required in certain cases.
They dispute a fish with an egg on it: Beit Shammai require two dishes, while Beit Hillel are satisfied with one.
Both agree that placing a cut-up egg or crushed leeks inside the fish makes two dishes.
Rava rules that halakha follows our mishna and Beit Hillel, so one dish suffices.
Quotes the mishna: if the eiruv food was eaten or lost, one may not cook for Shabbat with that initial intent.
Abaye states the tradition: one who began kneading on the Festival for Shabbat may finish baking if the eiruv was eaten.
Mishna: when the Festival follows Shabbat, Beit Shammai require immersing everything beforehand, while Beit Hillel require only vessels.
Both schools agree that impure water may be purified on Shabbat through a stone vessel, and that transfers between vessels or groups are allowed.
Gemara: everyone agrees that one may not immerse a vessel on Shabbat.
Asks the reason for this prohibition and which type of forbidden labor it involves.
Rabba says it is a rabbinic decree issued as a preventive measure.

18a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the decree's rationale: one might pick up the vessel and carry it four cubits in the public domain to immerse it.
Abaye asks: if one has a pit of ritually pure water in his courtyard, what is there to say?
Rabba replies that the decree covers a courtyard pit too, lest people treat it like a pit in the public domain.
Abaye challenges: this works for Shabbat, but on a Festival carrying between domains is permitted, so what is there to say?
Rabba replies that the Sages decreed against immersing on a Festival because of the Shabbat prohibition.
The Gemara objects: a mishna permits bringing impure water to pure water in stone vessels, so the same decree should apply there.
Rejects the objection: one with other pure water would not mix in impure water, so this is an exceptional case the decrees do not cover.
Abaye cites a baraita permitting drawing water with an impure pail on a Festival, and asks why the same decree does not apply.
Rabba replies: the pail is used only for drawing water, so the person remembers not to immerse it alone.
Abaye cites a baraita on vessels impure from the eve of a Festival, asking why the same decree does not cover those impure on the Festival.
Rabba replies that impurity arising on a Festival is rare, and the Sages did not decree against rare cases.
Abaye cites a baraita distinguishing primary and derivative impurity, and asks why the same decree does not apply.
Rabba replies that priests alone are careful about derivative impurity for teruma, so that case is rare and not decreed.
Rav Chiyya bar Ashi cites Rav: a menstruating woman with no clean clothes may immerse herself in her garments on Shabbat or a Festival.
Asks why the same decree should not forbid immersing the clothes, lest she immerse them alone.
Replies that she immerses them only while wearing them, so she remembers not to immerse them by themselves.
Rav Yosef holds that immersing vessels on Shabbat is decreed lest one wring them, a prohibited labor.
Abaye asks: this works for wringable vessels, but what is there to say about vessels that cannot be wrung?
Rav Yosef replies: the Sages decreed against unwringable vessels because of wringable ones.
Abaye raised all these same objections against Rav Yosef, to show that no such decree exists.
Rav Yosef answers as he did in Rabba's name.
Rav Beivai gives another reason: lest one delay immersing impure vessels until the Festival.
A baraita follows Rav Beivai: vessels impure on the eve of a Festival may not be immersed on the Festival, lest one delay.
Rava gives a further reason: immersing a vessel on Shabbat looks like repairing it.
Replies that by the same logic a person immersing himself appears to be cooling off, not purifying.
Objects: that works for pure water, but what is there to say if the ritual bath water is murky?
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak replies that a person sometimes bathes for other reasons, so intent to purify is not proven.

18b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Continues the example: one washes in hot weather even in putrid water, because the heat is uncomfortable.
Objects: this works in summer, but in the rainy season people do not bathe to cool off, so what is there to say?
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak replies that one sometimes comes home from the field muddy and soiled, and bathes even in the rainy season.
Objects: this explains bathing on Shabbat, but on Yom Kippur, when all bathing is forbidden, what is there to say?
Rava replies that Yom Kippur cannot forbid what Shabbat permits; since Shabbat permits it, Yom Kippur permits it too.
Asks whether Rava accepts the principle of since, given the contrary mishna.
Cites the mishna on sipping vinegar for toothache, and a baraita permitting sipping and swallowing, as contradicting the ruling.
Abaye resolves the contradiction: the mishna addresses sipping and spitting out, not swallowing.
Rava resolves it: the baraita permits sipping before dipping, while the mishna forbids sipping after dipping, when it is clearly medicinal.
Objects: if Rava accepts since, he should permit sipping after dipping too, since sipping before dipping is permitted.
Replies that Rava retracted that view on vinegar and accepted Abaye's resolution.
Asks how we know he retracted that view, perhaps only regarding immersion on Yom Kippur.
Rejects that: a baraita teaches that immersions are performed as usual on the Ninth of Av and Yom Kippur, so Rava would follow it.
The mishna: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that impure water may be brought into contact with pure water in stone vessels.
Asks what the mishna means by however one may not immerse the impure water.
Shmuel says one may not immerse an impure vessel for the sake of its water in order to purify it on a Festival.
Asks whose opinion the mishna follows, since it fits neither Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi nor the Rabbis.
A Tosefta: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi forbids both immersing the vessel for its water and bringing impure water into a stone vessel.
The Rabbis permit both: immersing the vessel for its water and bringing impure water into a stone vessel.
Asks which view the mishna follows, since each opinion seems to conflict with one of the two rulings in the mishna.
The mishna may follow Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, with the baraita's first clause about a Festival and its second about Shabbat.

19a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Offers an alternative reading: the mishna follows the Rabbis, and the whole mishna concerns Shabbat, when impure vessels may not be immersed.
A baraita: an impure vessel from the eve of a Festival may not be immersed at twilight, since its day status is uncertain.
Rabbi Shimon Shezuri says that even on a weekday one may not immerse at twilight, since the vessel needs a full sunset.
The first tanna does not require sunset to pass for the vessel's purification, so twilight immersion is allowed on a weekday.
Rava reports that the Sages of Rav's school disagreed over whether intention can be inferred from one's actions.
Asks what the circumstances of this dispute are.
Example: one runs with a vessel in hand at twilight to immerse it, so the action reveals the intention.
The Rabbis hold that running shows he knows sunset is needed and will wait a day, so twilight immersion on a Festival eve is forbidden.
Rabbi Shimon Shezuri holds that he may be running due to unfinished work, so the Sages decreed against any twilight immersion.
Rava explains that all agree intention can be inferred from actions, and they differ only in the particular case that follows.
The example: a vessel touched by a creeping animal smaller than a lentil, and its owner asks the Sages whether that imparts impurity.
Rabbi Shimon Shezuri reasons that one who does not know the lentil rule may not know the sunset rule either, so he is restricted.
The Rabbis permit weekday immersion: he may not know the lentil rule, but he knows sunset is required, as stated in the Torah.
Recalls the mishna: one may immerse on a Festival from one group to another, or from one principle to another.
A baraita explains: one may re-immerse vessels for a changed purpose, such as a winepress or another group's offering, since that immersion is not obligatory.
The mishna: Beit Shammai allow bringing peace-offerings but not burnt-offerings, while Beit Hillel allow both and permit laying hands on them.
Ulla limits the dispute to Festival peace-offerings regarding laying hands, and to the burnt-offering of appearance regarding sacrifice.
Beit Shammai read the verse about keeping the festival to permit peace-offerings on the day, but not the burnt-offering of appearance.
Beit Hillel read the phrase to the Lord as covering anything offered to the Lord, so it may be sacrificed on the Festival.
Ulla holds that vow- and freewill offerings may not be sacrificed on a Festival, and that all agree, including Beit Hillel.
Rav Adda bar Ahava likewise holds that vow- and freewill offerings may not be sacrificed on a Festival.
Raises an objection from a baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: the two schools agree on which offerings may and may not be sacrificed on the Festival.
Asks: with what, then, did they disagree?
They dispute the Festival burnt-offering and non-Festival peace-offerings: Beit Shammai forbid bringing them, Beit Hillel permit.
Resolves the contradiction by emending the baraita so that the dispute concerns only the Festival burnt-offering of appearance.
Rav Yosef replies that this is a dispute among tanna'im, so the objection was never a real difficulty.
Quotes another baraita on Festival peace-offerings: Beit Shammai lay hands on them the eve and slaughter on the Festival; Beit Hillel do both on the Festival.

19b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ulla and Rav Adda bar Ahava hold that vow- and freewill offerings may not be sacrificed on the Festival day itself.
The Gemara says these tanna'im resemble earlier tanna'im who disagreed on the same issue.
A baraita: a thanks-offering may not be brought on Passover because of its leavened bread, nor on Shavuot, but it may be brought on Sukkot.
Rabbi Shimon reads the verse on the three Festivals to mean that offerings valid on Passover are valid on the others, and the rest are not.
Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon says a thanks-offering may be brought on Sukkot and fulfills the joy obligation, though not the Festival peace-offering.
Asks what is surprising: obviously a thanks-offering with leavened bread cannot be brought on Passover.
Rav Adda bar Ahava, or Rav Shmuel bar Abba, explains: the case is Passover eve, since consecrated offerings may not be brought where eating time is restricted.
Explains that the tanna prohibits vow- and freewill offerings on a Festival, which is why thanks-offerings are excluded on Shavuot.
The baraita continues: a person may bring his thanks-offering on Sukkot.
Asks which Sukkot: if on the Festival day itself, that conflicts with the Shavuot ruling, so it must mean the intermediate days.
Rabbi Shimon's view repeated: offerings allowed on Passover are allowed on the other Festivals, and the rest are not.
Rabbi Zeira objects: if kindling wood is permitted on intermediate days, vow-offerings surely are, so Rabbi Shimon cannot forbid them.
Abaye: everyone agrees they may be sacrificed on intermediate days; the dispute concerns when the prohibition against delay applies.
The first tanna holds that the Torah lists three Festivals even out of order, so three passing Festivals trigger the delay prohibition.
Rabbi Shimon holds that the delay violation arises only if the three Festivals pass in their proper order.
Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon says a thanks-offering may be brought on Sukkot.
Asks when: on intermediate days it matches the first tanna, so it must mean the Festival day, where vow-offerings are permitted.
Asks why Sukkot is singled out as the example.
Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon follows his own consistent line of reasoning about the prohibition against delay.
A baraita: the verse names Sukkot last to teach that it is the final Festival for the delay prohibition, in the proper order.
Rabbi Elazar says Sukkot is named because that Festival itself causes a person to be late in fulfilling his vow.
A thanks-offering on Sukkot fulfills the joy obligation but not the obligation of a Festival peace-offering.
Asks why this is stated, since obviously an obligatory offering must come from unconsecrated animals.
Answers that it is needed for a case where one specified that the thanks-offering would also count as a Festival peace-offering.
Recalls Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish's question to Rabbi Yochanan about a thanks-offering vow that would also discharge a Festival peace-offering.

20a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether one may shave and buy nazirite offerings with second-tithe money.
Rabbi Yochanan replies that one who vows naziriteship may not shave and buy offerings with second-tithe money.
Case: a man instructs his agents to give four hundred zuz to a named man, on condition that he marry his daughter.
Rav Pappa rules that he takes the money, but may choose whether or not to marry the daughter.
Explains the difference: when the money is mentioned first, marriage is not a binding condition; reversed wording makes the money conditional.
Mareimar teaches this ruling in his own name, without attributing it to the Sage who stated it.
Ravina objects: we teach it as a question that Reish Lakish asked of Rabbi Yochanan, so the attribution matters.
A baraita derives from the verse on Aaron's burnt-offering that an obligatory burnt-offering also requires laying hands, like a gift offering.
Rabbi Yitzchak explains that this follows Beit Shammai, who do not derive obligatory peace-offerings from gift ones, so the verse is needed.
Asks how we know Beit Hillel derive obligatory peace-offerings from gift ones, rather than from obligatory burnt-offerings.
Challenges: gift peace-offerings are more common and may differ, so Beit Hillel should not learn from burnt-offerings either.
Answers that the halakha is derived from both sources together, so the argument gives no proof for Beit Hillel's position.
Beit Shammai hold that obligatory peace-offerings do not require the placing of hands.
Objects with a baraita of Rabbi Yosei: the schools disagreed only about slaughter immediately after placing hands, not about the placing itself.
Answers that the mishna follows the view of this baraita's tanna, on which the dispute concerns the placing of hands itself.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda: the schools agree slaughter follows hand-laying, but dispute whether hand-laying is required for obligatory peace-offerings.
A baraita recounts Hillel the Elder's burnt-offering on a Festival; Shammai's students challenge it, and Hillel claims it is a female peace-offering.
Shammai's school gains the upper hand and seeks to establish its view as halakha.
A disciple of Shammai, Bava ben Buta, knows the halakha follows Beit Hillel and sends word.

20b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Beit Hillel's side wins the custom of laying hands on offerings, and the halakha is fixed their way.
Narrative: a Beit Hillel disciple brings his offering on a Festival and meets a Beit Shammai disciple.
The Beit Shammai disciple challenges the laying of hands: what is this?
The Beit Hillel disciple turns the challenge back with a rebuke: what is this silence?
The Beit Shammai disciple falls silent under the rebuke and leaves.
Abaye's rule: a scholar should not answer a colleague's insult with a sharper reply.
Abaye supports the rule from the story, where the exchange repeats the same wording.
A baraita records Beit Hillel arguing with Beit Shammai about offerings on a Festival.
Beit Hillel's a fortiori argument: if Shabbat-forbidden offerings may be slaughtered on Shabbat for the Most High, then Festival-permitted ones may be too.
Beit Shammai reply that vows and gifts refute the argument, since they are permitted to commoners but barred to the Most High.
Beit Hillel says vows lack a fixed time, but the appearance offering has one, so the comparison fails.
Beit Shammai hold that the appearance offering also lacks a fixed time.
Beit Shammai cite a mishna: one who missed the first Festival day may keep celebrating through the last day.
Beit Hillel reject that claim and hold that the appearance offering does have a fixed time.
Beit Hillel cite a mishna: if the whole Festival passed without the offering, no obligation remains.
Beit Shammai cite a verse: only what every soul eats may be prepared for you, not for the Most High.
Beit Hillel answer with a verse on offerings to the Lord, and ask what the word for you then adds.
What does the verse's word for you come to teach?
It teaches that the rule covers Israel and excludes gentiles and dogs, not the offerings themselves.
Abba Shaul restates Beit Hillel's position in different words.
Abba Shaul's a fortiori argument from the open and closed stove and the full and empty table.
The Gemara asks what the two positions on vows and gifts on a Festival actually disagree about.
Rav Huna says that by the view that vows and gifts may not be sacrificed on a Festival, they are barred.
Rav Huna rejects the reading that the bar is only rabbinic, holding it is a Torah-level bar.
Rav Huna proves it from the Shavuot loaves, which are fixed to that day yet still do not override Shabbat or Yom Tov.
A dilemma: if one slaughtered vows and gifts on a Festival, what must be done with the blood?
Rava holds the blood is sprinkled to permit the meat to be eaten.
Rabba bar Rav Huna holds the blood is sprinkled to burn the fats and parts on the altar at night.
The Gemara asks what practical difference lies between these two views.
The difference appears if the meat became impure or was lost: Rava would not sprinkle, Rabba bar Rav Huna would.
An objection from a baraita on the Shavuot lambs, which are sprinkled and eaten even when slaughtered wrongly, but not on Shabbat.

21a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita: sprinkling after the fact is valid, but sprinkling ab initio on a Festival is not.
The baraita works for Rava but is difficult for Rabba bar Rav Huna, so the Gemara objects to him.
Alternatively, a Shabbat prohibition differs from a Festival one, since the Sages were stricter about Shabbat.
Rav Avya asks Rav Huna whether a jointly owned animal may be slaughtered on a Festival.
Rav Huna answers that it is permitted.
Rav Avya challenges him: how does this differ from vow-offerings and gift-offerings?
Rav Huna deflects the challenge by pointing at a passing raven, avoiding a reply.
Rabba, son of Rav Huna, asks why his father dismissed so great a scholar in that manner.
Rav Huna explains he was exhausted by communal burdens and needed time to reason the question.
The Gemara asks what the reason for the difference is.
A jointly owned animal can be slaughtered since an olive-bulk requires slaughter, unlike offerings that belong wholly to God.
Rav Ḥisda rules that a jointly owned animal may be slaughtered on a Festival, since an olive-bulk requires slaughter.
Rav Ḥisda rules that jointly owned dough may not be baked on a Festival, since it can be divided during kneading.
Rav Ḥana bar Ḥanilai objects with a mishna permitting baking of dog-food dough on a Festival.
The Gemara asks why that dough may be baked, since it could be divided during kneading.
Dog-food dough differs because the owner can appease the dogs with a carcass.
The Gemara challenges Rav Ḥisda's view on since, citing the dispute over one who bakes on a Festival.
Rav Ḥisda holds that one is flogged and Rabba holds not, based on their views of the since principle.
The Gemara retracts the prior answer: the case must be one where a carcass is already ready.
Residents are asked whether they may bake flour supplied to gentile soldiers on a Festival.
Rav Huna rules it depends on whether the soldiers let the villagers give bread to a child.
A baraita on Shimon the Timnite, who slaughtered a calf to placate soldiers, is cited against the lenient ruling.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava rebukes him that his loss from desecrating the Festival outweighed his gain.
He supports this with a verse: food may be prepared for you, not for gentiles.
The Gemara asks why the calf was forbidden, since part of it was fit to eat.
Rav Yosef says the calf was a tereifa, a non-kosher animal that could not be eaten by Jews.
The Gemara objects that the calf was still fit for dogs, so it could be slaughtered for them.
The dispute over labor for dogs on a Festival is a dispute between tanna'im.
A baraita derives from the verse that even an animal's soul is included, so the words for you exclude such labor.

21b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The verse for you and not for dogs is cited as the source for the dispute.
Rabbi Yosei the Galilean's position is set against Rabbi Akiva's view that even an animal's soul is included.
If so, what does the repeated word for you come to teach?
It shows the verse excludes gentiles, not dogs.
Why include dogs and exclude gentiles, instead of the reverse?
Dogs are included because their food is provided by you, while gentiles are excluded because their food is not.
Abaye tells Rav Yosef that Rabbi Yosei the Galilean holds the verse excludes dogs from the rule.
How may they carry these feeds for animals on a Festival?
Rav Yosef says they are fit for fuel, so carrying them is allowed.
Abaye objects: fuel suffices for dry matter, but what can be said about wet matter?
Rav Yosef replies that they are fit for large fuel as well.
The same objection is raised about Shabbat, asking what can be said.
They may be carried along with the bread.
Shmuel's principle: a person may do all his needs with bread.
This is disputed by Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who permits inviting a gentile on Shabbat but not on a Festival.
Rav Aha bar Yaakov holds that even on Shabbat the reason is not leftover cups.
If so, our cups are fit for hens too, and theirs as well, so why may they be carried along with a cup?
Rava says one may carry a jar with its lid, since the case differs because the cup itself is forbidden for benefit.
Rav Aha of Difti asks Ravina whether the item would be like a dung vessel.
Ravina replies that one would never make a dung vessel to begin with.
Rava reports Shmuel's teaching: inviting a gentile is allowed on Shabbat but not on a Festival, a decree lest one add more.
Marimar and Mar Zutra tell a gentile visitor on a Festival that they will bear the extra trouble only if he agrees.
The Mishnah: Beit Shammai forbid warming water for one's feet unless drinkable, while Beit Hillel permit a bonfire for warming.
Is the bonfire ruling agreed by all, and does Beit Shammai distinguish warming the whole body from one limb?
A Mishnah shows Beit Shammai forbid a bonfire warming, while Beit Hillel permit it.
The Mishnah: Rabban Gamliel is stringent in three matters, covering warming, lamp-raising, and thin wafers.
Rabban Gamliel says his father's household baked only thin wafers.
They reply to Rabban Gamliel: his father's household was strict on itself yet lenient for all Israel, so they may bake thick bread.
What is the reasoning when one has set up an eruv of cooked foods, and when one has not?
Rav Huna says the case is one who did not set up the eruv, and the Sages permitted him enough for his life.
Rav Huna's own ruling supports this: one who did not set up an eruv may bake one loaf and cook one pot.

22a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yitzchak permits lighting a lamp and roasting a small fish for one who did not set up an eruv of cooked food.
A baraita is cited to the same effect.
The baraita lets such a person bake one loaf, bury one pot, light the lamp, and heat one jug.
Some say roasting a small fish is also permitted for him.
Rava says the case is one who did set up an eruv; burying is different because the intent for Shabbat is evident.
Abaye objects with a baraita of Hananiah.
Hananiah's baraita reports Beit Shammai's rulings on baking, cooking and burying hot water before the Festival.
Even though the intent for Shabbat is evident, the Gemara questions the ruling's basis.
Abaye explains the case as one who prepared for one person but not for another, and the view is Beit Shammai's.
The Mishnah adds that one may not raise the lamp.
The Gemara asks what the phrase means.
It concerns a lamp of rings, which looks like building; Beit Shammai hold building applies to vessels, Beit Hillel do not.
Ula visited the house of Rav Yehuda and raised a lamp.
Rav Yehuda objects that one who pours oil into a lamp is liable for kindling, and one who draws from it for extinguishing.
Ula replies that he did not do it intentionally.
Rav rules that hemp may be used.
Abba bar Marta asks Abaye whether one may extinguish a lamp because of another matter.
Abaye asks whether it is possible to act in another house.
No other house, no partition, no covering of the vessel, and no vessel is available.
Abaye rules that it is forbidden.
A baraita permits extinguishing a coal only to spare it, or to keep the house or pot from smoking.
Abaye says that is Rabbi Yehuda's view, while he speaks for the Sages.
Abaye asks Rav Marin whether one may extinguish a Festival flame where life is at risk.
Rav Marin replies that it is forbidden.
The same baraita about extinguishing a coal is raised again as an objection.
That is Rabbi Yehuda's view, while he speaks for the Sages.
Rav Ashi asks Amimar whether one may apply eye salve on a Festival where there is danger.
Amimar replies that it is forbidden.
A baraita is cited that one may not extinguish a coal.
Amimar taught the case differently: applying salve through a gentile on Shabbat is permitted.
Some report that Amimar himself applied salve through a gentile on Shabbat.
Rav Ashi challenges Amimar with Ula's view that all needs of a sick person may be done through a gentile on Shabbat.
Rav Hamnuna rules that one may tell a gentile to do anything not life-threatening, but only where one does not help in the act.
The qualification is challenged: the Master does help, as Rav Zavid stands beside him.
The reply is that such assistance is not substantive.
Amimar permits applying eye salve on the second day of Rosh Hashana.
Rav Ashi challenges Amimar.
Rava's ruling is cited: if one dies on the first Festival day, gentiles prepare the body, and Israelites on the second, even across two Rosh Hashana days.

22b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: What is the difference from the case of an egg?
The speaker follows the Nehardea view, which applies the same rule to an egg.
Perhaps they intercalate Elul to make the festival fall in another month?
Rav Chinena bar Kahana states that since Ezra's time Elul was never intercalated.
One may bake only thin wafers, not thick bread.
A baraita: Beit Shammai forbid baking thick bread on Passover, while Beit Hillel permit it.
How thick must bread be to count as thick bread?
Rav Huna says a handbreadth, as the showbread was a handbreadth thick.
Rav Yosef objects that the measure would be wrong in every other respect, such as oven and fuel.
Rav Yirmiya asks Rav what thick bread means.
Rav answers that thick bread means bread in large quantity.
Rav Yirmiya reports Rav's teaching that thick bread is bread in large quantity.
Why is it called thick bread?
Because much kneading is involved.
Alternatively, in the region of this tanna, large bread is called thick bread.
Since the name would then refer to unnecessary trouble, the reason seems unsatisfying.
Why does the baraita mention Passover in particular?
Yes, it applies to other festivals too, but the tanna speaks of Passover.
A baraita states the same: Beit Shammai forbid baking large bread on a festival, Beit Hillel permit it.
The Mishnah: the same authority permits three things: clearing the bed-chamber, placing incense, and roasting a kid on Passover eves.
Rav Asi explains that the dispute concerns incense for smoke, but for scent everyone agrees it is permitted.
A baraita objects that the bed-chamber may not be cleared on a festival, yet Rabban Gamliel's household did.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Tzadok recounts repeatedly seeing Rabban Gamliel's household prepare the room the day before.
If so, the Sages argue that it should then be permitted on Shabbat as well.
The same baraita on incense and Rabban Gamliel's household, with Rabbi Eliezer ben Tzadok's account of preparing the day before.
If so, the Sages argue that it should then be permitted on Shabbat as well.
Rav Asi's teaching is restated: the dispute is only for scent, while for smoke it is forbidden.
May one produce smoke on a festival?
Rav Yirmiya bar Abba says Rav holds it is forbidden.
Shmuel permits it, while Rav Huna forbids it because it extinguishes.
Rav Nachman asks why not say the reason is that it kindles.
Rav Huna replies that its beginning extinguishes and its end kindles.
Rabbi Yehuda rules that one may not do this on a live coal.

23a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Placing an item on a potsherd is permitted.
Rabba holds that placing an item on a potsherd is also forbidden, because it produces smell.
Rabba and Rav Yosef both hold that a cup may not be left on a hot place on a Festival, since it gives off smell.
What is the reason, and how does this differ from the case of smelling a cut or uprooted item?
There the item adds smell, while here it produces smell, so the cases differ.
Rava holds that placing an item on a live coal is also permitted.
Rava argues by analogy to roasting meat in embers, and cites Rav's practice at the house of the Exilarch.
Ameimar asks what qitura, the incense, means.
If qitura is a craftsman's act, then if it is for smoke it is forbidden, since it extinguishes.
Rav Ashi replies that in general it is for smoke, like roasting meat in embers, and some say so.
Ameimar repeats the challenge: if qitura is a craftsman's act, then smoke is forbidden since it produces smell.
Rav Ashi says he taught it as a generic rule, that smoke is permitted like roasting meat in embers.
The Mishnah permits making a roasted kid.
Rabbi Yosei relates that Todos of Rome taught Roman citizens to eat a roasted kid on Passover eves, and the Sages objected.
The Mishnah: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya permits three things, which the Sages forbid, including leading a cow out by a strap and combing or grinding on a Festival.
Rabbi Yehuda permits scraping but not combing, while the Sages forbid both.
The Gemara challenges whether Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya had only one cow, which would make the ruling about combing odd.
Rav says Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya tended thirteen thousand calves, and the cow was merely borrowed from a neighbor.
Combing is permitted on a Festival.
A baraita defines combing and scraping: minors may comb and form a group, adults may scrape but not form a group.
Rabbi Yehuda holds that a non-intended act is forbidden.
Minors may comb and form a group, while adults may scrape, and we do not decree scraping because of combing.
The Sages agree that a non-intended act is forbidden and decree scraping because of combing; Rabbi Elazar follows Rabbi Shimon, and both are permitted.
Rava reports Rav Nachman's ruling, following Shmuel, that the halakha is as Rabbi Shimon holds.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya concedes to this view.
Rava challenges Rav Nachman to rule that the halakha is as Rabbi Yehuda, since the Sages concede to him.
Rav Nachman replies that he holds like Rabbi Shimon, and that Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya concedes to him.

23b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Mishnah: a millstone of peppercorns is impure because of three vessels, the receptacle, the metal vessel and the sieve.
The tanna explains which vessel is at fault: the lower stone for the receptacle, the middle for the sieve, the upper for metal.
The Mishnah: a child's cart is impure as a seat of ritual impurity and may be carried on Shabbat, but may be dragged only on vessels; Rabbi Yehuda extends this to all vessels except the cart.
The Gemara explains that the cart is impure because the child sits on it, so it counts as a vessel, and it cannot be dragged on the ground.
What is the reason the cart may not be dragged on the ground?
Because dragging it on the ground makes a furrow.
The tanna is Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that a non-intended act is forbidden.
If it were Rabbi Shimon, who permits non-intended acts, the reasoning fails, as the Mishnah shows.
Rabbi Shimon permits dragging a stool and bench, provided one does not intend to make a furrow.
The Gemara instructs that one should read the latter clause instead.
Rabbi Yehuda rules that all items may be dragged on Shabbat except the cart, because it presses down.
Making a furrow is not done; the two tanaim disagree, and the view is Rabbi Yehuda's.
The chapter closes with the formula that concludes this chapter of tractate Beitzah.
The Mishnah: one may not hunt fish from pools on a Festival or give them food, but may hunt beasts and birds from pools and feed them; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules otherwise.

24a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A principle: a thing that still needs trapping is forbidden on a Festival, one that does not is permitted.
A Mishnah on pools of beasts and birds seems to contradict the principle: hunting from pools is forbidden, and feeding them too.
The contradiction is restated: beasts against beasts, and birds against birds.
Beasts against beasts is no difficulty, since the cases are about different tanaim.
One is Rabbi Yehuda and the other is the Sages, as we learned in a Mishnah.
Rabbi Yehuda holds that one who hunts a sparrow into a tower or a deer into a house is liable, but not for a pool.
The Sages hold that a sparrow into a tower, and a deer into a courtyard or pool, is permitted.
Birds against birds is still a difficulty, and the proposed resolution is raised and rejected.
The case is a covered pool against an uncovered one, and a house counts as a covered pool.
Both Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages agree that a sparrow may be taken to a tower but not to a house.
Rabba bar Rav Huna says the case is about the dror sparrow, which does not obey its owner and lives in a house like a field.
Beast against beast is also no difficulty: one case is a small pool, the other a large one.
What do a small pool and a large pool look like?
Rav Ashi defines them: where prey can be caught in one pool and the other in the second pool, or where the pools are adjacent.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says not all pools are alike.
Shmuel rules that the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
Abaye objects that the halakha ruling implies a dispute, so the Gemara must treat them as disagreeing.
What difference does it make to you?
The Gemara is complete, so the twig you are stuck with can be used as a stick; a dismissive reply.
The principle again: whatever needs trapping is forbidden, and so on.
What does it mean that something needs trapping?
Shmuel says it is anything where one can say: bring a net and we will catch it.
Abaye objects with geese and hens, which can be said of, yet a baraita exempts them.
Rabba bar Rav Huna cites Shmuel: these come to their pen at night, and those do not.
Doves in a dovecote and doves in an upper room come to the pen at night, yet a baraita holds one liable for taking them.
Shmuel's distinction: these come to their pen at night and their food is upon you, while those do not come and their food is not upon you.
Rav Mari says some are apt to multiply and some are not, and the rule speaks of those apt to multiply.
The Mishnah: a Festival hunt prepared the day before may not be taken from unless one knows it was caught before the Festival, with a gentile's fish story to illustrate.
The story is brought to explain the Mishnah's wording: in doubt, a prepared item is forbidden.
Rabban Gamliel permits such fish, which supports the view that the case is permitted.
Shmuel says the halakha is not like Rabban Gamliel, and some teach the Mishnah in line with a baraita where Rabban Gamliel permits and Rabbi Yehoshua forbids.
Shmuel rules the halakha follows Rabbi Yehoshua, and some teach it in line with the baraita.

24b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Mishnah permits slaughtering from the carpenters' lumber on a Festival, but not from nets or traps.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: if game was found spoiled, it is permitted when known to be caught before the Festival, forbidden when caught on it.
The ruling itself is difficult.
If the case is game found spoiled and known to be caught before the Festival, the reason must be that in doubt it is forbidden, which would conflict with the ruling.
Instead, the Gemara says to read the latter clause.
The Gemara restates the latter clause: in a doubtful case it is treated as caught on the Festival and so forbidden.
Shmuel rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, and the game is permitted.
For what purpose is the game permitted?
Rav says it is permitted for receiving, while Levi says it is permitted for eating.
Rav teaches that a person should never keep himself from the study house, even for one hour.
Rav and Levi heard the same ruling from Rabbi: in the evening he said permitted for eating, in the morning permitted for receiving, and Levi did not return to the house.
A baraita objects: a gentile who brings a gift to a Jew, even split fish or fruit of yesterday, is permitted.
This fits the view that it is permitted for receiving, but not the view that it is permitted for eating, since fruit of yesterday may not be eaten.
By your view, fruit of yesterday would be permitted for carrying.
The case is about bundles of fruit and produce that were pickled in vegetables.
Why then does the baraita call them yesterday's fruit?
Because they resemble yesterday's fruit.
Rav Pappa rules: if a gentile brings a Jew a gift on a Festival and it is of a kind still attached to the ground within the boundary, it is forbidden; the same applies at night.

25a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Something outside the boundary is forbidden.
An item brought for one Jew is permitted for another Jew.
Rabba bar Rav Huna reports Rav's ruling: one who cleared a water channel on the eve of a Festival and found fish in the morning may use them.
Rav Hisda teaches from our Rabbis that a bird nesting in an orchard does not need summoning.
Rav Nachman gives a variant attribution of the same teaching, from Rabba bar Rav Huna.
Rav Nachman distinguishes: there no act was done, while here an act is done and no summoning is needed.
A baraita says a bird nesting in an orchard needs summoning, and Shemaiah and Avtalion's testimony is cited against the view.
A baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree on one who summoned within the nest, and which birds need the ring.
The baraita continues: attached birds in pits, houses and bushes may be used.
The baraita continues: attached birds in trees are forbidden lest one pluck them, and attached birds anywhere are forbidden as theft.
Rav Nachman resolves the contradiction by distinguishing mother and ring cases, and Rabbi Nachman bar Yitzchak distinguishes gardens near a town from those far from it.
The Mishnah: one may not slaughter a dangerous animal unless there is time to eat a kazayit of roast meat by day; Rabbi Akiva allows even raw meat near the place of slaughter.
Rami bar Abba derives from the Torah the good conduct that one may not eat meat before it is flayed and cut up, and the same for butchers.
What then does this teach us to exclude?
Perhaps it excludes Rav Huna's view that a living animal is presumed forbidden until one knows how it was slaughtered.
But we learned in a Mishnah that the rule follows Rav Huna.
Rabbi Akiva's ruling: one may eat a raw kazayit from the place of slaughter itself.
The Gemara asks whether the phrase means literally the place of slaughter, and answers that it does not.
But Rabbi Chiyya teaches that it means the place of slaughter itself.
Rami bar Abba's view is set out, to be continued.

ranges.en: The derekh eretz rule is taught here as a matter of courtesy.
A baraita: one should not eat onion and garlic at the head of a table, and gulping a cup at once marks one as a glutton.
Rami bar Abba lists the lowering of certain people's standing, including the wicked, the butchers, and the cursed of Israel.
He cites a verse about Israel serving the Baalim and abandoning God as the source for this list.
The phrase they forsook God is read with its implications, to show they did not serve Him.
Why does the verse add that they did not serve Him?
Rabbi Elazar teaches that God said: even this lupine, boiled seven times and eaten, is not made to serve them.
Rabbi Meir teaches why the Torah was given to Israel: because they are fierce.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael cites a verse about the fiery law given from His right hand.
Some say the fire of the other nations' laws is such that no nation could stand before Israel without the Torah.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish: three things are fierce, Israel among nations, the dog among animals, the rooster among birds, and some add the goat and the caper.
The Mishnah clause on slaughtering in the field and not bringing the animal on a pole.
A baraita: a blind person may not go out with his stick, nor a shepherd with his satchel, and a man and a woman may not go out with one cup.
The Gemara objects: but Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi sent a case of an old man who went out with his sandal.
The old man asked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who ruled that if many need it, it is permitted.
The Sages relied on the words of Achi Shakya, who said he brought Rav Huna a cloth from one fold to another.
Rabbi Nachman bar Yitzchak says he brought Shmuel a cloth from one place to another, and the reason is that if many need it, it is permitted.
Rav Nachman tells a messenger how Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi died while carrying a cup and seated himself; the anecdote shows the practice.
Rabbi Ami is cited: one may carry it provided he does not carry it on the shoulder.
What does the proviso that one not carry it on the shoulder mean?
Rav Yosef the son of Rava rules that one may carry on a stretcher.
The Gemara objects: but Rav Nachman permitted a Festival stretcher to go out.
That case is different: the stretcher was used because of fear, and some say because of the people's crowding.
The Mishnah: if a firstborn fell into a pit, Rabbi Yehuda says a skilled person should descend and check.

26a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Mishnah: if a firstborn has a blemish one may bring it up and slaughter it, and if not, one may not slaughter it.
Rabbi Shimon: an animal whose blemish is not visible before the Festival does not count as prepared.
In what do the two Tannaim disagree?
Perhaps they disagree about whether blemishes may be seen on a Festival, not about blemishes in general.
The case of a firstborn that fell into a pit is needed to teach that the Sages did not let him leave it for concern for animal suffering, and so one may bring it up as Rabbi Yehoshua holds.
If so, the Mishnah should have said not slaughter and not bring up, instead of bring up and slaughter.
The case is where it fell and was brought up, and the teaching is that one may slaughter it.
This is not a tam, since the case concerns one in which a blemish fell on it.
But the animal is muktzeh, so it could not be handled on the Festival.
Rather, the case is where a blemish came on it before the Festival eve.
Now the blemish is permanent; the teaching is needed lest one think his intent covers slaughtering it, and it is taught so.
A baraita: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says a skilled person should descend into the pit and check; if there is a blemish, it may be brought up and slaughtered.
Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya objects: they said blemishes are not seen on a Festival, so how is a blemish that arose before the Festival to be checked?

26b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Shimon holds that an animal whose blemish is not visible before the Festival does not count as prepared.
The Mishnah agrees that if a blemish was born with the animal, it counts as prepared.
Rabba bar Rav Huna teaches that if the blemish was born with it, one may check it on a Festival, initially.
Rav Nachman objects: a baraita says if one passed and checked, the check was valid, yet you say checking is initially permitted.
Abaye rules with Rabba bar Rav Huna, as the Mishnah's three clauses make clear.

The Mishnah's three clauses: a blemish arising before the Festival may not be checked initially, but after the fact it is fine; a blemish arising on the Festival is not prepared even after the fact, per Rabbi Shimon.
The Mishnah's other clause: if the blemish was born with it, it counts as prepared even initially.
Rav Oshaya brings a baraita saying that whether the blemish arose before or on the Festival, the Sages hold it is not prepared; the Gemara finds this difficult.
That baraita is by Ada bar Ukhmi, who errs and teaches incorrectly; Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says the Mishnah is precise.
The Mishnah is precise: Rabbi Shimon says whoever's blemish is not visible before the Festival is not prepared.
What does it mean that the blemish is not visible? If it means not visible at all, that is obvious.
It means not visible to a sage before the Festival eve; from this we learn that the matter is not prepared, and Hillel asks Rava.
Hillel asks Rava whether there is muktzeh for half of Shabbat, and asks what the case looks like if visible at twilight.
Rava says there is muktzeh.
A Mishnah clause is raised as an objection: why not say this firstborn was visible with its mother and then born, so it was pushed aside and shown to a sage and permitted?
Abaye, or Rav Safra, says the case is where judges sat, and some say he told him there is muktzeh for half of Shabbat.
Shall we say it supports him?
The same objection is restated about the firstborn visible with its mother and permitted after being shown to a sage.
Abaye, or Rav Safra, says the case is where judges sat.
A baraita: one who ate grapes and left some on the roof to make raisins, or figs for dried figs, may not eat them unless he invited them before dusk; the same applies to apricots and other fruits.
What is the case: if they were visible, why is an invitation needed; and if not visible, what does an invitation do?
If you say he does not know whether they were visible, but Rav Kahana said that muktzeh which dried up and whose owners do not recognize it is permitted.
Rav Kahana rules that dried-up muktzeh that owners do not recognize is permitted.
Rather, isn't it that they were visible, pushed aside, then visible again; and if there is no muktzeh, why the invitation? So there is muktzeh.
If he invites them, what happens?
The case is needed where they were visible and not visible: some people eat and some do not.
If he invites them, his intent is revealed; if he does not invite them, his intent is not revealed.
Rabbi Zeira teaches the halakha as a further proof.
Come and hear: beans and lentils were visible at first to be cooked, and then were pushed aside into the pot.

27a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Some items were already cooked and visible before the Festival.
Abaye objects: by your reasoning, ordinary pots are hot at twilight and one eats from them at night.
The difference is between what is finished by human hands and what is finished by heavenly hands.
Rabbi Yehuda the Nasi had a firstborn that he sent to Rabbi Ami, who thought it should not be shown.
The halakha is according to Rabbi Yehuda, as stated by Rabbi Zeira or Rabbi Yirmiya.
The firstborn is sent to Rabbi Yitzchak the smith, who also held it should not be shown, and the halakha is according to Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Abba asks what the reason is for not letting the Sages act on the view of Rabbi Shimon, and asks what he has in hand.
Rabbi Zeira said so.
The halakha is according to Rabbi Shimon: a man went up there to learn the teaching from the mouth of his teacher.
Rabbi Zeira says he does not reason it that way, but from the Mishnah.
The Mishnah has Rabbi Shimon's view that one whose blemish is not visible before the Festival is not prepared, and a baraita uses the language of the Sages.
So it follows that the reasoning is in accordance with Rabbi Shimon.
What is the upshot of this?
Rav Yosef said so.

A baraita transmitted from Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul and the holy community of Jerusalem: Rabbi Shimon and his colleagues ruled the halakha like Rabbi Meir.
But they were much older than him, so why would they rule like him?
They ruled it according to Rabbi Meir's system.

A Mishnah: one who slaughtered a firstborn and then showed its blemish, Rabbi Yehuda permits, while Rabbi Meir forbids since it was slaughtered without an expert; so Rabbi Meir holds that seeing a firstborn is not like seeing a treifa.
Rabbi Meir's distinctions: seeing a treifa after slaughter, and seeing a firstborn before the Festival, are each valid.
Abaye objects: is it the same there, where the blemishes are seen and the dispute is over the fine?
Rabba bar bar Chana cites Rabbi Yochanan: where the examined animals are all agreed, the prohibition is because they change; the dispute concerns blemishes in the body.
Rabbi Meir holds that we decree blemishes in the body because of blemishes that are visible, while Rabbi Yehuda holds we do not decree.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says the Mishnah is precise: Rabbi Meir says that since it was slaughtered without an expert, it is forbidden, which shows it is a fine; and an anecdote about Rabbi Ami of Vardina and the Nasi's firstborn not seen o
Is it so? But Rabbi Ami himself saw it, and when he saw, it had been seen the day before.
