ranges.en: On the Festival, the question is asked: how was the case?
A man brought a firstborn before Rava on an eve of a Festival; Rava saw its blemish, told him to come back, and the next day asked how it happened.
Rava asks again how the case went.
The man explains that barley was spread on one side while he was on the other, and that the blemish was caused by his own act, which is forbidden.
A baraita: a blemish must not be in it, and beyond that it must not be caused by another means, such as letting a dog take the dough, so the verse says every blemish.
The Mishnah: a dead animal may not be moved from its place; Rabbi Tarfon was asked about it and about the consecrated loaf that became impure, and he said it may not be moved.
Shall we say the Mishnah is anonymous and not like Rabbi Shimon?
Rabbi Shimon says one may cut pumpkins before the animal, and the carcass before the dogs.
Rabbi Yehuda says that if it was not a carcass before Shabbat, it is forbidden.
Even if you say Rabbi Shimon agrees, he held that dead animals are forbidden.
Mar bar Amemar, citing Rava, says Rabbi Shimon agrees that dead animals are forbidden, which is fine.
Mar, son of Rav Yosef, citing Rava, says Rabbi Shimon distinguishes, so that even dead animals are permitted.
What can be said?
Ze'iri's version: the Mishnah speaks of holy animals, and the reason is holiness; common animals are permitted.
Granted, according to Mar, son of Rav Yosef, citing Rava, Rabbi Shimon distinguishes, so dead animals are permitted.
Alternatively, according to Mar bar Amemar citing Rava, Rabbi Shimon agrees that dead animals are forbidden.
Here we speak of a dangerous animal, on which all agree.
The Mishnah: one may not count the animal's share on a Festival initially, but may do so the eve before, and slaughter and divide.
What does not counting mean?
Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel: one may not initially divide the money on the animal on a Festival.
How does one manage this on a Festival?
Rav says one brings two animals and places them side by side, and says this one is like that one.
A baraita so teaches: one may not say to a fellow I am with you for a sela, or two; one may say I am with you for half, a third, or a quarter.

28a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Mishnah: Rabbi Yehuda says one may weigh meat against the vessel or the cleaver, while the Sages say one does not pay attention to the scale-pan at all.
What does at all mean?
Shmuel holds it means even to guard the meat from mice, and Rav Idi bar Avin says the case is one hung on a hook.
Shmuel rules that a butcher may not weigh meat by hand, and may not weigh it in water.
Rav Chiyya bar Ashi forbids making a handle in the meat, Ravina permits it with the hand, and Rav Huna permits marking the meat.
Rabba bar Rav Huna, cutting it into three corners as a mark, shows the practice.
Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi weigh a mina against a mina on a Festival, following which view?
If it is Rabbi Yehuda's view that one weighs meat against the vessel, then against nothing else; and if the Sages, they say one does not pay attention to the scale-pan at all.
A baraita: Rabbi Yehoshua says one may weigh a mina against a mina on a Festival.
Rav Yosef rules the halakha follows Rabbi Yehoshua, since the Mishnah on firstborns follows that view.
Abaye objects: perhaps Rabbi Yehoshua speaks only where there is no disrespect to the sacred items, but where there is disrespect, no.
Alternatively, the Sages speak only because it does not look like weekday work, while here it looks like weekday work.
Does this mean they were particular with each other? But these women came to the house of Rabbi, and five of them were in Rabbi Chiyya's house, and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi was not particular.
Rav Pappa says someone threw a man between them, so they were not particular.
The Mishnah: one may not sharpen a knife on a Festival, but one may place it on the other one.
Rav Huna says this applies only to a stone whetstone; a wooden one is permitted.
Shmuel clarifies: the stone prohibition applies to sharpening, but removing grease is permitted; so a wooden one is permitted even to sharpen.
Some teach the final clause of the Mishnah as wood permitted, and then Shmuel clarifies: removing grease is permitted, sharpening is forbidden, and stone is forbidden even to remove grease.
Some teach the Mishnah itself: one may not sharpen a knife on a Festival; Shmuel says sharpening is forbidden but removing grease is permitted, so even placing one on another is permitted.
Some teach the final clause: Shmuel clarifies that sharpening is forbidden and removing grease permitted, so with a whetstone even removing grease is forbidden.
Which tanna holds that a whetstone is forbidden?
Rav Hisda says it is not like Rabbi Yehuda, as a baraita teaches: between Festival and Shabbat, only food preparation is permitted, while Rabbi Yehuda permits even tools for food.
Rava says to Rav Hisda: we teach in your name that the halakha is like Rabbi Yehuda.
Rav Hisda replies: may it be that you teach from me only the good things; my teachings are not to be taught that way.
Rav Nachmiah, son of Rav Yosef, reports standing before Rava and seeing how he acted.

28b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Anecdote: a teacher seen running a knife on a Festival says it is only for removing fat, while the narrator sees he is sharpening.
Abaye reports a parallel case with Rabba, who also claimed fat removal while holding that sharpening is the halakha but not publicly taught.
Is it permitted to show a slaughtering knife to a Sage on a Festival to check it for nicks?
Rav Mari son of Rav Bizna permits it, the Rabbis forbid it, and Rav Yosef says a scholar may check a knife privately and lend it.
Rav Yosef rules a blunt knife that still cuts may be sharpened on a Festival, but one that cuts no longer may not.
Rav Ḥisda's cases of nicked knives, broken skewers and oven sweeping raise the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis.
A baraita: only food preparation differs between Festival and Shabbat, and Rabbi Yehuda permits even auxiliary acts for food preparation.
What is the reason of the first tanna for forbidding actions that facilitate food preparation?
The verse Only what every person must eat may be done for you is read as excluding the means of preparing food.
Rabbi Yehuda reads the verse For you, for all your needs, to include auxiliary actions needed for food preparation.
Doesn't the first tanna also have For you written, and what does that phrase teach him?
The first tanna's For you teaches that the Festival rule applies to Israelites, not to gentiles.
Doesn't Rabbi Yehuda also have the limiting word That written, alongside For you, so how can both be read?
No contradiction: the prohibition covers tasks that can be done on the eve, while tasks that cannot be done on the eve are allowed.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel: a bent roasting skewer may not be repaired on a Festival.
Isn't this obvious, since one may plainly not repair a utensil on a Festival?
No, it is needed for a case where the skewer can be straightened by hand, which is still forbidden.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel: a skewer on which meat was roasted may not be moved on a Festival.
Rav Adda bar Ahava, citing Rav Malkiyu: one may pull the skewer aside into a corner so it does not endanger anyone.
Rav Ḥiyya bar Ashi, citing Rav Huna: this applies only if the skewer still has an olive-bulk of meat on it.
Ravina disagrees: even without an olive-bulk of meat, the skewer may be moved in the regular manner into a corner.
Ravina supports this by analogy to a thorn lying in the public domain, which may be removed for public safety.
Rav Ḥinnana son of Rav Ika reports three rulings of Rav Malkiyu on skewers, maidservants and follicles, and three of Rav Malkiya on forelocks, ashes and cheese.
Rav Pappa's principle: rulings tied to a mishna or baraita are Rav Malkiya's, and others are Rav Malkiyu's, with a mnemonic.
What is the practical difference between Rav Ḥinnana's view and Rav Pappa's view?
The practical difference concerns the halakha about maidservants, which Rav Ḥinnana attributes to Rav Malkiyu and Rav Pappa to Rav Malkiya.
Mishna: one may not ask a butcher on a Festival to weigh a dinar's worth of meat, but he may slaughter and divide without stating a price.
What should one do in a case like this, where one wishes to take part of an animal but may not mention its price?

29a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Local idioms in Sura, Neresh, Pumbedita and Mata Meḥasya for asking a butcher for a portion without naming a price.
Mishna: one may ask a neighbor to fill a vessel on a Festival but not by measure; Rabbi Yehuda is stricter, and Abba Shaul's grocery practice is described.
What does the phrase 'but not by measure' in the mishna mean?
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel: only a vessel designated for measuring is barred, and Rabbi Yehuda extends the ban even to vessels that could measure.
Apparently Rabbi Yehuda is stricter on Festival joy, while the Rabbis are lenient, in this matter?
But we have heard the opposite, so the mishna's stance on weighing meat contradicts this understanding.
The mishna cited: Rabbi Yehuda lets a person weigh meat against a vessel or cleaver, while the Sages say one may not look at the scale.
The two statements of Rabbi Yehuda, and of the Rabbis, appear to contradict each other, so the positions seem reversed.
No contradiction: each case differs in whether the vessel is designated for measuring, and whether the act resembles a weekday activity.
Rava offers a second explanation.
What does 'but not by measure' mean on Rava's reading?
It means one may not name a measure to the seller; a vessel designated for measuring may still be filled without naming one.
Rabbi Yehuda comes to say one may not fill a vessel designated for measuring even when no particular measure is stipulated.
Apparently Rabbi Yehuda is stricter on Festival joy while the Rabbis are lenient, as before?
But we have heard the opposite in the mishna's weighing case, which contradicts this reading.
The mishna again cited: Rabbi Yehuda permits weighing meat against a vessel or cleaver, while the Sages forbid looking at the scale.
The statements of Rabbi Yehuda and of the Rabbis appear mutually contradictory, leaving their positions apparently reversed.
No contradiction: the vessel is not designated for measuring, and people commonly pour wine from measuring vessels for friends to drink.
The Gemara recalls the incident of Abba Shaul ben Botnit, a grocer who measured the evening before a Festival.
A baraita: Abba Shaul measured even on Festival intermediate days, to avoid neglecting Torah study in the study hall.
A baraita: Abba Shaul and colleagues gathered three hundred jugs of wine and oil and brought them to the Temple treasurers in Jerusalem.
The treasurers say such scruples are unnecessary, since buyers already allow for foam and residue; the grocers reply they will not benefit.
The treasurers tell them, since they are stringent with themselves, to use the goods for communal needs.
A baraita about one who stole and does not know the victim: he should use the goods for communal needs, supporting the treasurers' ruling.
What exactly are communal needs?
Rav Ḥisda: communal needs include financing the digging of cisterns, ditches and caves for storing water for travelers.
Rav Ḥisda authorized Rabbana Ukva to teach publicly, and he taught the following ruling on measuring grain for animals.
One may not measure barley and place it before an animal on a Festival, but one may cut a hole in the pile with a vessel and not worry.
A baker may measure spices and place them in the pot so the dish does not spoil, since too much would ruin the food.
Rav, citing Rav Yirmeya bar Abba: a woman may measure flour on a Festival to separate ḥalla generously.
Shmuel disagrees and says that such measuring is prohibited.
But a Sage of Shmuel's school taught a baraita stating that this measuring is permitted, contradicting Shmuel.
Abaye notes the conflict: Shmuel rules it prohibited, while the baraita of Shmuel's school permits it.

29b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Gemara explains that Shmuel restated the known baraita to teach the practical ruling.
Baraita forbids sifting flour a second time on a Festival.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira permits re-sifting, and the Sages agree with him.
All agree that removing a fallen pebble or chip after sifting is allowed.
A tanna taught before Ravina that one may pick out a pebble by hand.
Ravina objects that picking by hand is even more forbidden, since it resembles selecting.
Rava bar Rav Huna teaches at Neharde'a that re-sifting flour on a Festival is permitted.
Rav Nachman dismisses that teaching by pointing to how commonly sieves are already used.
Rav Yosef's wife sifts unusually, and his remark implies the practice is acceptable.
Rav Ashi's wife sifts onto a table, another practice that supports the permission.
Rav Ashi explains her practice is authoritative because she learned it from her pious father.
Mishnah permits asking a grocer for counted eggs and nuts on a Festival, since counting is not commerce.
Tosefta permits buying one kid, cut of meat, bird, or loaf from regular vendors on a Festival.
A grocer may be asked for a stated number of items, provided no measure is named.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar permits this too, provided the price is not mentioned.
Chapter-closing formula that also opens the next chapter of the tractate.
Mishnah forbids carrying many jugs in a basket on a Festival, but permits carrying them on the shoulder.

30a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna's tail: one may take straw from the straw pile but not wood set aside in storage.
Baraita: if the usual weekday way of carrying cannot be modified, the usual way is permitted.
Rava instituted graded carrying modifications in Mechoza, and they yield to impossibility.
Rav Chanan bar Rava says the Sages required modifying weekday methods on a Festival whenever possible.
Why are women filling jugs on a Festival without modifying, and why is no protest made?
It is impossible for them to fill any other way.
Switching jug sizes adds walking or extra load, so that alternative is also unworkable.
Covering the jug with wood or tying the cover risks forbidden handling or tying.
Spreading a scarf risks squeezing, so no modification is possible and the usual manner stays.
Rava bar Rav Chanin cites the mishna forbidding clapping, thigh-slapping and dancing on a Festival.
Why do women clap nowadays without any protest, if the mishna forbids it?
Abaye counters with Rava's ruling against sitting at an alley entrance, which women also ignore.
The principle is to leave Jews alone, so they sin unwittingly rather than deliberately.
Some limit the principle to rabbinic prohibitions and exclude Torah prohibitions.
No such distinction exists; the principle applies equally to Torah and rabbinic prohibitions.
The biblical extension of Yom Kippur is ignored by people eating until dark, proving the principle.
The mishna states that one may begin taking straw from the straw pile.
Rav Kahana infers that one may begin removing items from a storeroom on a Festival.
The mishna follows Rabbi Shimon, who does not hold that set-aside items are prohibited.
If so, the latter clause about wood storage would follow Rabbi Yehuda, who holds muktze.
The wood is cedar and fir, so its set-aside status stems from financial loss, which even Rabbi Shimon accepts.
Some teach Rav Kahana's point as applying to the latter clause about wood storage.
Rav Kahana reads the mishna as forbidding starting from a storeroom, which follows Rabbi Yehuda.
If so, the first clause about straw would follow Rabbi Shimon, who holds no muktze.
The straw in the first clause is rotted, so even Rabbi Yehuda would treat it as fuel.
Rotted straw is still fit for clay, so why assume it is used only as fuel?
The mishna refers to thorny straw, which cannot be kneaded into clay.

30b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: one may not take wood from a sukka on the Festival, only from wood placed beside it.
Why is taking wood from the sukka forbidden if taking from beside it also dismantles a tent?
Shmuel explains that beside means next to the walls, which are not part of the wood.
Rav Menashya qualifies that the baraita concerns reed bundles not yet untied, hence not roof.
A baraita taught before Rabbi Yochanan: one may not take wood from a sukka, only from nearby wood.
Rabbi Shimon permits taking from the sukka; all agree a festival sukka is off limits unless conditioned.
Taking wood from a sukka seems to dismantle a tent, so how can Rabbi Shimon permit it?
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: the case is a sukka already collapsing, so only muktze is at issue.
Rabbi Shimon rejects muktze, as a baraita on lamp oil permitting use shows.
The lamp case differs, since one can foresee the lamp going out but not the sukka falling.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: the case is a flimsy sukka, already in mind the day before.
All agree a festival sukka is forbidden, but conditions made on it are honored.
Can a condition even take effect on sukka wood, given Rav Sheshet's teaching in Rabbi Akiva's name?
Rabbi Akiva derives from the verse about seven days of the festival that sukka wood is prohibited all week.
A baraita of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira: sanctity of Heaven applies to the sukka as to the festival offering.
The repeated phrase for the Lord shows the sukka is consecrated just like the festival offering.
Rav Menashya bar Rava: conditions work on an ordinary sukka but not on a sukka of mitzva.
A Tosefta on decorations with conditions is cited, suggesting conditions work even for a sukka of mitzva.
Abaye and Rava: the Tosefta concerns decorations declared usable at once; sukka wood keeps its sanctity for seven days.
How does that differ from the case of setting aside etrogs, where sanctity does not carry over?
The case: one sets aside seven etrogs, one for each day of the Festival.
Rav holds one fulfills the obligation with each etrog and may eat it right away.
Rav Asi holds one may eat each etrog the next day, as its sanctity lasts through that day.
Etrog sanctity ends at each night since its mitzva is only by day, so each day stands alone.
Sukka's mitzva applies at night too, so the seven days form one continuous day.

31a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: wood may be brought from a field only if gathered, but from a karpef even scattered wood is allowed; defines karpef.
Rav Yehuda in Shmuel's name: wood may be brought only from gathered wood in a karpef.
The mishna itself permits bringing even scattered wood from a karpef, contradicting that ruling.
The mishna represents a single individual's opinion, not the accepted view.
A baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagreed only about scattered karpef wood and gathered field wood.
Beit Shammai forbid bringing gathered field wood, while Beit Hillel permit it.
Rava: reed and vine leaves are scattered by wind and forbidden, unless weighted down the day before.
The mishna's definition of a karpef is repeated.
Does Rabbi Yosei's key rule add to a karpef near a city, or only apply within the Shabbat limit?
Alternatively, Rabbi Yehuda may define any enclosure near a city as a karpef regardless of key, so what is Rabbi Yosei adding?
A mishna says Rabbi Yosei allows entry with a key even within the Shabbat limit, so both conditions are lenient.
The halakha follows Rabbi Yosei as a leniency, as Rabbi Yirmeya ruled.
Mishna: one may not chop wood on a Festival from beams or broken beams, or with an ax, saw, or sickle; only a cleaver. Gemara marker.

31b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Why does the mishna later permit chopping if its first clause forbids chopping beams at all?
Shmuel says the mishna is incomplete and must be read with its omitted words restored.
The restored mishna: no chopping from the beams pile or a beam broken on the Festival; only with a cleaver.
A baraita teaches the same rule, supporting the restored reading of the mishna.
Rav Chinnana bar Shelemya in Rav's name: only the female broad side of an axe is prohibited, not the narrow male side.
Obviously the narrow side of an axe is allowed, since the mishna permits a cleaver.
The ruling was needed because one might extend the cleaver prohibition to the axe side of a combined tool.
Another version teaches the same ruling about the latter clause, with the narrow side allowed and broad side forbidden.
Obviously the axe's broad side is forbidden, and the mishna forbids the axe; why teach the cleaver?
The ruling was needed because one might allow the narrow side of a combined tool by analogy to a cleaver.
Mishna: produce in a locked house may be taken through a hole; Rabbi Meir permits making a hole ab initio.
Why does Rabbi Meir allow making a hole, which seems to dismantle a tent?
Shmuel: the case is bricks stacked without cement, which is not a building at all.
Rav Nachman says bricks stacked in rows are set aside, so they remain muktze even uncemented.
Rabbi Zeira: Rabbi Meir speaks of a Festival, where the hole is permitted but not on Shabbat.
A baraita states that Rabbi Meir's leniency applies on the Festival but not on Shabbat.
Shmuel: one may untie but not unravel or cut knotted cellar fastenings on Shabbat, while vessel fastenings are allowed both days.
A baraita permits untying but not unravel or cutting ground fastenings on Shabbat, while the Festival allows all, contradicting Shmuel.
That baraita follows Rabbi Meir, while Shmuel follows the Rabbis who reject his leniency.
Do the Rabbis really dispute Rabbi Meir about ground-sealed doors?
A baraita reports the Sages concede to Rabbi Meir on ground-sealed doors, distinguishing Shabbat and the Festival.

32a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shmuel follows a tanna whose baraita permits untying ground fastenings and vessel fastenings differently on Shabbat and Festival.
Shmuel's ruling conflicts with the baraita, which forbids unraveling vessel ropes on Shabbat.
That baraita follows Rabbi Nechemya, who holds vessels are used only for their designated purpose.
If Rabbi Nechemya's view is the basis, why limit it to Shabbat, and is his distinction between Shabbat and Festival coherent?
Conflicting baraitot on whether vessels and their shards may be used for kindling are cited.
The baraitot reflect different tannaim: Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Nechemya, so they do not conflict.
Mishna: on a Festival one may not shape a lamp, make charcoal, or cut a wick; Rabbi Yehuda permits burning a wick.
Which tanna holds that hollowing a lamp creates a vessel, even before firing?
Rav Yosef: it is Rabbi Meir.
A baraita on ritual impurity: Rabbi Meir counts a clay vessel from when its work is complete, not after firing.
Abaye objects that Rabbi Meir may speak only of vessels able to hold liquids, not of a lamp.
A lamp can still hold small coins, so it counts as a vessel.
Some say that Rav Yosef holds the mishna follows Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Tzadok.
A mishna on ḥaraniyyot pots: Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Tzadok deems them vessels before firing, so they can contract impurity.
Abaye objects that Rabbi Eliezer may speak only of ḥaraniyyot pots, which can hold something.
A lamp can hold small coins.
The Sages taught that one may not hollow a lamp or make ḥaraniyyot pots on a Festival.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits making ḥaraniyyot pots on a Festival.
What does the word ḥaraniyyot mean?
Rav Yehuda: it means pots of a city.
What does the word ʿaraniyyot, a variant term, mean?
Abaye: villagers' bowls, which are not fully formed or fired and are used as they are.
It is obvious that charcoal is not permitted, since it serves no sustenance purpose; for what is it fit?
Rabbi Chiyya: the rule is needed for handing charcoal to bathhouse attendants for heating the same day.
Is it permitted to heat water on the Festival for washing?
Rava: the decree forbids entering a bathhouse only to sweat, and it predated the later decree on sweating.
Mishna: one may not cut the wick into two, though Rabbi Yehuda permits cutting it by fire.
What is different about cutting a wick with fire compared with a knife, that a knife is forbidden?

32b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Does cutting a wick by fire also mend a vessel, as the earlier objection assumed?
Rabbi Chiyya explains the cutting is done with the wick placed across two lamps being lit.
Rav Natan bar Abba in Rav's name: one may moḥet a wick on a Festival.
What does the term moḥet mean?
Rav Chanina bar Shelemya in Rav's name: it means removing the dark, burnt part to brighten the lamp.
Bar Kappara teaches six wick rules on a Festival, three stringent and three lenient.
The stringent rules: no spinning or twisting a wick, no singeing it before lighting, and no cutting it in two.
The lenient rules: crushing it by hand, soaking it in oil, and cutting it by fire between two lamps.
Rav Natan bar Abba in Rav's name: wealthy Babylonian Jews will go to Gehenna for lacking compassion, illustrated by Shabbetai bar Marinus.
Deuteronomy 13:18 shows that those lacking compassion cannot be descendants of Abraham.
Rav Natan bar Abba in Rav's name: one who depends on others' tables finds the world dark.
Job 15:23 describes the dependent man, whose day of darkness is ready at hand.
Rav Chisda: such a person's life is not really life.
A baraita lists three whose lives are not lives, including one dependent on others' tables, and some add one with a single robe.
The first tanna excludes the single-robe man because he can examine his clothes and remove lice.
Mishna: one may not break earthenware or cut paper to roast salted fish on a Festival.
Mishna: one may not sweep out an oven's fallen debris, though one may press down the ashes.
Mishna: one may not join two barrels to hold a pot, prop a pot, or lead an animal with a stick; Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon permits the last.
What is the reason for prohibiting breaking earthenware and cutting paper?
Because one thereby prepares a vessel for use.
Mishna: one may not sweep out an oven or stove on a Festival.
Rav Chiyya bar Yosef taught before Rav Nachman that sweeping is permitted if baking is otherwise impossible.
Rav Chiyya's wife's oven was blocked by a brick, and he told her he wanted good bread, implying the sweeping was permissible.
Rava told his attendant to roast a duck carefully, implying impediments may be cleared to avoid singeing.
Ravina asks why Rav Ashi's servants may plaster an oven's mouth on a Festival without it being kneading.
Rav Ashi: one relies on riverbank mud already kneaded, and Ravina adds that ashes may be used since kneading does not apply to them.
Mishna: one may not join two barrels to hold a pot.
Rav Nachman: lavatory stones may be arranged on a Festival for use.
Rabba objects that joining barrels to hold a pot is forbidden, implying building-like arrangements are prohibited.
Rav Nachman replies that barrels differ because the arrangement forms a tent-like covering.
Rabba the Younger asks whether a built bench with no gap underneath would also be permitted by the same logic.
Permanent building is forbidden by Torah, temporary building only by rabbinic decree, and the lavatory's dignity is not subject to that decree.
Rav Yehuda: a bonfire built top-down is permitted, while one built bottom-up, like a house, is forbidden.

33a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Similar rule for placing eggs, a pot, a bed or barrels: hold the upper piece first, then place the rest below.
Can a pot really be propped against a door? Better to correct the wording to a door propped by wood.
Corrected wording: one may not prop a door with a piece of wood either.
Baraita: one may not prop a pot with wood, since wood is only for kindling, though Rabbi Shimon permits it.
One may not lead an animal with a stick on a Festival; Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon permits it.
Does Rabbi Elazar follow his father, who denies muktze, and so permits any stick?
No: even Rabbi Shimon agrees here, because leading the animal with a stick looks like going to market.
Rav Nachman forbids a bamboo skewer as muktze and Rav Sheshet permits it; the dispute concerns dry branches.
Each side's reasoning: wood is only for kindling versus wood may be used for roasting in any manner.
An alternate version: dry branches are permitted and wet ones forbidden, which is the halakha.
Rava: one may not take a firebrand from a wood store, and a broken firebrand may not be kindled, since it was once a vessel.
Does Rava hold Rabbi Yehuda's muktze view, given his other ruling?
Rava told his attendant to throw duck innards to the cat, which Rabbi Yehuda would forbid as unprepared.
The innards were already rotting and set aside the day before, so they were prepared.
Mishna: Rabbi Eliezer permits taking a splinter from a straw pile and kindling straw from the courtyard.
The Sages permit collecting only from items placed before him in the house, not from the courtyard.
Mishna: one may not make fire by rubbing wood, striking stones or tiles, or using water and sun, nor whiten tiles hot for roasting.
Gemara opens: Rav Yehuda said, beginning a new statement.

33b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Fodder such as straw and reed branches carries no prohibition of preparing a vessel, so it may be trimmed on Shabbat.
Rav Kahana objects with a baraita on spice-tree wood that seems to forbid cutting wood to smell it, contradicting Rav Yehuda.
Rav Yehuda replies that the baraita must be read as referring to hard wood, which is the difficulty.
The baraita is incomplete: soft spice wood may be cut and smelled, but hard wood may not be cut.
Two conflicting baraitot: one permits cutting and smelling spice wood, the other forbids it.
Rav Chisda's resolution: the permitted case is soft wood and the forbidden case is hard wood.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov objects that hard wood should be no different from breaking a barrel to eat figs.
The mishna permits breaking a barrel to eat figs, provided one does not intend to make a vessel.
Rava bar Rav Adda and Ravin add that Rav Yehuda cut hard spice-wood sticks for them, which seems permitted.
Not difficult: that case follows Rabbi Eliezer and this case follows the Rabbis.
Baraita: Rabbi Eliezer permits taking a toothpick from before oneself, and liability for plucking it is described; the Rabbis differ.
The Rabbis treat both cases as only rabbinic, so cutting spice wood to smell is permitted ab initio according to them.
Does Rabbi Eliezer reject the barrel-and-figs mishna, which allows breaking a barrel without intent to make a vessel?
Rav Ashi: the lenient case concerns a vessel already patched with pitch, so breaking it does not make a vessel.
Mishna: one may collect straw from the courtyard on a Festival.
Baraita: one may collect from the courtyard and kindle, as long as not in piles; Rabbi Shimon permits even piles.
What is the basis of the dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi Shimon?
The Rabbis fear appearing to gather for later days, while Rabbi Shimon notes the pot shows the intent is cooking.
Mishna: one may not bring out fire, and so on.
What is the reason for forbidding bringing out fire?
Because one thereby creates something new on the Festival.
Mishna: one may not whiten tiles by heating them to roast on them.
What is one doing with the whitened tiles, if the purpose is only roasting?
Rabbi Yochanan: the case concerns new tiles, which are forbidden because they must be prepared first.

34a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The reason for the restriction is the need to test new vessels or harden them, which counts as preparing a vessel.
A mishna on a fowl trampled or crushed: if it survives twenty-four hours and is slaughtered, it is kosher, but must still be examined.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira whether slaughtering such a bird is permitted on a Festival.
Rabbi Zeira cites the mishna forbidding whitening tiles to roast on them, as a parallel case.
Rabbi Zeira's reason is the need to harden the tiles to make them vessels, not to examine them, so the parallel does not apply.
Baraita: several people can jointly cook on Shabbat and all are liable, since each contributes a part of the act.
A different baraita says only the last person is liable and the rest exempt, conflicting with that.
The cases differ: when fire was brought at the outset everyone contributed, but when brought at the end, the earlier ones did nothing.
Granted all perform cooking, what prohibited labor does the one who places the pot on the stove perform?
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish: the case is a new pot, which takes on the prohibition of strengthening it, like new tiles.
Tosefta: new ovens and stoves may be used like vessels, but not oiled, rubbed or cooled to harden them, except to bake on the Festival.
Tosefta: on a Festival one may scald and singe an animal's head and feet to remove hair, but not smear or shear them.
Tosefta: one may trim certain vegetables and bake in a large oven, but not in a new oven that might crack.
Tosefta: one may not blow fire with bellows but may use a tube, nor mend or sharpen a skewer.
Tosefta: one may not split a reed for a skewer, but may crack a nut wrapped in a rag.
Mishna: Rabbi Eliezer adds a leniency: one may stand over stored objects that were set aside from use.

34b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna on the Sabbatical eve: one may eat from fruit set aside without tithing, though the Sages require marking the pile first.
Two mishnayot cited: children who hid figs before Shabbat must tithe before eating, and one who gathers figs in a courtyard is exempt.
Does Shabbat establish an obligation to tithe food whose preparation is unfinished, as it is a delight?
Rav Nachman: Shabbat establishes tithing obligation for items whether or not their preparation was finished.
Rava suggests Shabbat should mirror a courtyard, establishing tithing only for items whose preparation was completed.
Rav Nachman: this is an established teaching we hold, that Shabbat applies to both kinds of items.
Mar Zutra cites the mishna of Rabbi Eliezer on the Sabbatical eve, supporting Shabbat establishing tithing obligations.
Mar Zutra reasons that the Sabbatical year differs only because it is exempt from tithes, so other years are forbidden too.
Is the reason not that Shabbat establishes the produce as tithable?
There it differs: declaring one will eat from it tomorrow establishes the meal, so the produce is set aside.
If so, why specify Shabbat, since the same would apply on a weekday?
The mishna teaches that untithed produce is not inherently muktze but is prepared for Shabbat, so correcting it by tithing suffices.

35a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If the leftovers are returned to the pile, how can declaring intent establish the food as tithable, given Rabbi Eliezer's view?
Mishna in Ma'asrot: one who dips olives from a vat one at a time pays no tithe, while ten set out at once are tithable; Rabbi Eliezer distinguishes pure and impure vats.
What is the difference between the first and latter clause of that mishna, and why does purity matter?
Rabbi Abbahu: the first clause concerns a pure vat and impure person who cannot return olives, while the latter concerns impure olives that can be returned.
But the olives are returned and left in place, so the proposed explanation cannot stand.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi: Rabbi Eliezer's view is that separating teruma makes fruit fixed, so Shabbat, a stronger case, does too.
The mishna's latter clause: a declaration the day before is not enough unless one marks the pile and says from here to there.
The reason the Sabbatical eve is special is that the fruit is not subject to tithes, while other years' fruit is forbidden.
Is the reason not that Shabbat itself establishes the fruit as fixed?
No: that case differs, since declaring he will eat from here to there tomorrow already fixes the meal.
If so, why specify Shabbat when the same would apply on a weekday?
The mishna teaches that untithed produce is not muktze but is prepared for Shabbat, so tithing it after the fact corrects it.
A baraita on eating a grape cluster as one enters a courtyard or Shabbat begins: Rabbi Eliezer allows finishing, Rabbi Yehoshua does not.
Rabbi Natan: Rabbi Eliezer's leniency means exiting the courtyard or waiting until Shabbat ends, so there is no contradiction.
Rabbi Yochanan: Shabbat, teruma, a courtyard, or a sale establish tithing only for items whose preparation is completed.
Shabbat excludes Hillel's view, which prohibits eating fruit gathered on Shabbat until tithes are separated; Rabbi Yochanan rejects that.

35b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The courtyard rule is needed to exclude Rabbi Yaakov's view, as the mishna on figs taken into a courtyard shows.
Baraita: Rabbi Yaakov obligates such figs for tithes and Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda exempts them, while teruma is excluded from fixing fruit.
Mishna: fruit from which teruma was separated before completion is forbidden by Rabbi Eliezer for casual eating, but permitted by the Sages.
Baraita on figs bought from an am ha'aretz: they may be eaten casually until completed, then tithed as doubtful produce.
Three inferences from that baraita: a sale fixes produce only when work is complete, most am ha'aretz tithe, and doubtful produce may be tithed.
Rabbi Yochanan rules against the mishna on exchanged fruit, following the view that a sale fixes fruit only when work is complete.
Colophon marking the end of the chapter and the start of the next.
Mishna: on a Festival one may lower drying produce through a skylight, but not on Shabbat; one may cover produce and place a vessel under a leak on Shabbat.
Rav Yehuda and Rav Natan read the opening word differently, mashilin or mashchilin, and Mar Zutra says both are valid.
Mar Zutra: each reading has a valid basis in its own usage.
Deuteronomy 28:40 uses the root for fall, supporting the reading mashilin.
A mishna on the shachul and kasul blemishes uses the root sh-ch-l for slipping out of place, supporting mashchilin.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: other variants, mashirin, mashchirin and manshirin, are also valid.
A mishna on a nazirite and the root for causing hair to fall supports mashirin.
A mishna on the shachor razor supports mashchirin.
A mishna on clothes that fell into water, and on gleaning that falls during harvest, supports manshirin.
Mishna: one may lower produce through a skylight on a Festival; the question is how much.
Rabbi Yochanan: the limit is four or five sacks, as allowed for visitors or to preserve Torah study on Shabbat.
Perhaps there it is different, since there the mitzva of hospitality or Torah study is at stake, which is absent here.
Alternatively, Shabbat is weightier and so the limit applies there, while the lighter Festival might be treated lightly.
Alternatively, the limit on Shabbat reflects that no monetary loss is involved, whereas loss here permits moving more.

36a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The earlier mishna says one may not clear out a whole storeroom while removing sacks.
Shmuel: not clearing the whole storeroom avoids exposing the floor and levelling its depressions.
Is clearing produce from a roof on a Festival also forbidden if it exposes the floor, and does Shabbat or the Festival govern?
Mishna: one may lower produce through a skylight on a Festival.
Rav Nachman: that ruling applies only within the same roof, not moving produce from one roof to another.
A baraita confirms: one may not carry from one roof to another even when they are level.
Is moving sacks on Shabbat between roofs or houses forbidden, and is that stricter than the Festival case?
A baraita: one may not lower produce by rope through windows or by ladders on the Festival.
Would moving sacks on Shabbat by rope or ladder be permitted, given the Festival rule, and is it stricter or lighter?
Mishna: one may cover produce against a leak.
Ulla: covering extends even to bricks; Rabbi Yitzchak: only items fit for Festival use, since a vessel may be handled only for a handleable purpose.
The mishna's example of covering produce, not bricks, is offered as support for Rabbi Yitzchak.
No proof: the first clause already mentions produce, so the latter clause's produce example is only parallel, not exclusive.
Mishna: one may similarly cover jugs of wine and oil against a leak.
Those jugs hold untithed produce, which is muktze, so bricks would be treated the same.
If the jugs held permitted liquid, the first clause already covers produce, so why mention them?
The jugs teach that small losses, not only large ones, may be prevented by covering.
Mishna: one may place a vessel under a leak on Shabbat.
The leaking water is fit to be drunk, at least by animals, so it is usable.
A baraita permits spreading a mat over bricks on Shabbat, which contradicts Rabbi Yitzchak.
That baraita concerns leftover building bricks that are fit to chill drinks on.
A second baraita permits spreading a mat over stones on Shabbat, which are muktze.
Those are rounded stones fit for lavatory use, so they are not muktze.
A baraita permits covering a beehive with a mat, though bees and the hive are unfit for Shabbat use.
The baraita's rule: a mat may cover a hive against sun or rain, as long as one does not intend to trap the bees.
The hive contains honey, which is edible on Shabbat, so the mat is handled for its sake.
Rav Ukva asks Rav Ashi what applies in the rainy season, when there is no honey.
The baraita concerns the two honeycombs left for the bees, which are muktze unless the beekeeper intended to eat them.
The case is one where the beekeeper had intended beforehand to take the honeycombs.
If he had no such intent, why not state the rule in terms of intent, rather than trapping the bees?
Even if he intended to take the honeycombs, covering is permitted provided he does not intend to trap the bees.
If the baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda and the latter clause follows Rabbi Shimon, it is internally inconsistent.
Abaye and Rava say Rabbi Shimon forbids even unintended harm where the act inevitably kills, so Rabbi Shimon cannot be the source.
Rabbi Yehuda throughout: the hive has side windows, so trapping is not inevitable and the intent clause is relevant.

36b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Reading the baraita as forbidding trapping bees on Shabbat, since it would otherwise seem permitted as a non-typical hunt.
Rav Ashi: the baraita refers to spring and autumn, when there is sun or rain and honey in the hive.
Mishna: one may place a vessel beneath a leak on Shabbat to catch the water.
Baraita: if the vessel fills, one may pour it out, return it, and repeat without hesitation.
Abaye's mill leaked on Shabbat; Rabba advised treating the dirty water as excrement so it could be removed.
Abaye doubts whether one may deliberately create a situation requiring removal of excrement.
Abaye's mill then collapsed, which he took as punishment for not following Rabba's ruling.
Shmuel: containers of excrement and urine may be removed on Shabbat, but must be refilled with water before returning.
Some understood Shmuel to allow removing excrement only together with its container.
A dead mouse in Rav Ashi's spice store was removed directly by the tail, refuting that understanding.
Mishna: acts liable on Shabbat for rabbinic, optional, or full mitzva reasons are also liable on a Festival.
Mishna lists rabbinic-decree acts: climbing a tree, riding an animal, swimming, clapping, and dancing.
Mishna lists acts for optional mitzvot: judging, betrothal, halitza, and levirate marriage.
Mishna lists acts for full mitzvot: consecrating, valuations, dedications, and separating teruma and tithes.
Those acts are prohibited on a Festival too; the only difference from Shabbat is preparing food.
Climbing a tree is forbidden as a decree lest one detach leaves, which is reaping.
Riding an animal is forbidden as a decree lest one go beyond the Shabbat limit.
Does this show that the Shabbat limit is biblical, since the decree would not be needed if it were rabbinic?
Rather, the riding decree is to prevent cutting a switch, which is biblically forbidden reaping.
Swimming is forbidden lest one make a flotation barrel, a kind of improvised device.
Clapping and dancing are forbidden lest one craft a musical instrument.
Mishna: judging is an optional mitzva, not a full one.
Why is judging optional rather than a full mitzva, since judging is itself a mitzva?
The mishna speaks of a case where a more qualified person is available, so it is not an absolute mitzva.
Why is betrothal optional, since it fulfills the mitzva of being fruitful and multiplying?
The mishna needs to categorize it as optional for the same reason.

37a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Those with a wife and children have fulfilled the mitzva, so halitza and levirate marriage are optional acts for them.
But isn't performing halitza or levirate marriage a full mitzva?
The case is one with an older brother, whose levirate marriage is preferred, so the younger brother's act is optional.
The reason for all these prohibitions is a decree lest one write a document, such as a verdict or a deed.
Mishna: consecrating, valuations, and dedicating objects to the Temple are full mitzvot but are forbidden on Shabbat and Festival.
These are prohibited as a decree because they resemble commerce, which is forbidden on a Festival.
Mishna: one may not separate terumot and tithes on a Festival either.
Is it not obvious that separating teruma is forbidden as a labor of making forbidden food usable?
Rav Yosef: the mishna is needed to forbid separating teruma even to give it to a priest the same day.
That applies to produce that was untithed the day before; produce made on the Festival, such as dough for challah, may be separated and given to a priest.
Are the optional and mitzva categories not rabbinic shevut, since the mishna names only the first category as shevut?
Rabbi Yitzchak: all are prohibited as shevut, the mishna's wording only ranks increasing notability.
Mishna: all these acts are forbidden on a Festival, a fortiori on Shabbat.
A mishna permits lowering produce through a skylight on a Festival but not Shabbat, which contradicts the claim that food preparation is the only difference.
Rav Yosef: the two mishnayot follow different tannaim, Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua.
A baraita on a cow and calf in a pit on a Festival: Rabbi Eliezer's view limits raising the animals.
Rabbi Yehoshua's view in that baraita permits raising both animals to prevent loss.
Abaye asks how Rav Yosef knows Rabbi Eliezer's limit, since the pit case allows sustenance but the roof case does not.
Alternatively, Rabbi Yehoshua's leniency may be limited to cases where artifice is possible, which the roof case lacks.
Rav Pappa: the mishna follows Beit Shammai, while the other follows Beit Hillel.
Mishna: Beit Shammai forbid taking out a child, lulav, or Torah scroll on a Festival, while Beit Hillel permit it.
Perhaps Beit Shammai only forbid transferring between domains, not moving items within the house.
Moving items within a house is also done for carrying out, so the decree covers it too.
Mishna: animals and vessels follow the owner's limits, or the borrower's, depending on who controls them.
Mishna: a borrowed vessel follows the borrower's limits if borrowed before the Festival, and joint ingredients follow both parties; Rabbi Yehuda exempts water.

37b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objection that the mishna's ruling contradicts Rabbi Dosa's view on animals delivered to a shepherd on the Festival eve.
A baraita is brought, stating Rabbi Dosa's ruling that an animal sold or delivered before the Festival takes its owner's resting place.
Reply that the mishna can follow Rabbi Dosa too, since the baraita concerns one shepherd and the mishna two shepherds.
Rabba bar bar Hana reports Rabbi Yohanan's ruling that the halakha follows Rabbi Dosa on this matter.
Objection: Rabbi Yohanan elsewhere ruled that the halakha follows the anonymous mishna, which says the animal stays the owner's.
Resolution: the baraita and the mishna address different cases, one shepherd versus two shepherds, so no contradiction arises.
A baraita describes two partners who borrowed one robe, with Shabbat limits placed in different directions and the robe restricted accordingly.
An amoraic dispute: Rav holds the barrel is permitted but the animal forbidden, while Shmuel holds the barrel is forbidden too.
What is Rav's reasoning, and does his view depend on whether one accepts retroactive designation (berurah) or not?
Rav holds there is retroactive designation, but animals differ because their limits draw nourishment from each other, so the portions stay mixed.
Rav Kahana and Rav Asi object that the Sages were lenient about muktze yet strict about Shabbat limits, which seems illogical; Rav is silent.
What was the final conclusion on this issue?
Rabbi Hoshaya holds there is retroactive designation, while Rabbi Yohanan holds there is none.
Does Rabbi Hoshaya really hold that retroactive designation applies?
A mishna about a corpse in a house with many entrances is cited, seemingly showing Rabbi Hoshaya rejects retroactive designation.
The tannaim dispute the mishna's rule: Beit Shammai require the intention before death, Beit Hillel accept intention even after death.
Rabbi Hoshaya explains that Beit Hillel's ruling applies only from the moment of intention forward, not retroactively.
Resolution: reverse the attributions, so Rabbi Hoshaya denies retroactive designation and Rabbi Yohanan accepts it.
Objection: Rabbi Yohanan's ruling that brothers who divided an inheritance are purchasers from each other shows he rejects retroactive designation.
Explanation: Rabbi Yohanan rejects retroactive designation only in Torah law, but accepts it in rabbinic matters such as Shabbat limits.
Does Rabbi Yohanan really accept retroactive designation in rabbinic matters?
A baraita of Rabbi Yehuda, who forbids a person to stipulate on two contradictory conditions, contradicts that acceptance of retroactive designation.

38a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Why would the case of two rabbis at two locations differ from the single-rabbi case, if both lack retroactive designation?
Rabbi Yohanan explains the first case as one where the rabbi already arrived, and Rabbi Hoshaya, not Rabbi Yohanan, accepts retroactive designation in rabbinic matters.
Mar Zutra taught publicly that the halakha follows Rabbi Oshaya on retroactive designation.
Shmuel rules that an ox of a fattener is as the feet of any buyer, while a shepherd's ox is as the feet of the local townspeople.
The mishna teaches that a vessel borrowed from another on the Festival eve is as the feet of the borrower.
Is this not obvious, since the vessel's resting place is already in the borrower's possession?
The ruling is needed for a vessel not yet delivered until the Festival, lest one think it stays as the lender's feet.
The mishna supports Rabbi Yohanan's statement that a vessel borrowed on the Festival eve, even if delivered only on the Festival, is as the borrower's feet.
The mishna teaches that a vessel borrowed on the Festival itself is as the feet of the lender.
Is this not obvious as well?
It is needed for a borrower who regularly borrows from this lender, since the lender may still seek someone else and so keeps the object until handed over.
The mishna adds that a woman who borrowed spices, water or salt from another for her dish or dough has them as the feet of both.
Rabbi Abba came from Babylonia to Eretz Yisrael and found the sages discussing the mishna's rule about the dough.
Why is this the halakha for dough? Should the water and salt not be considered nullified, following the flour rather than the minor ingredients?
Rabbi Abba responded to the sages and began to answer their question.

38b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A case is presented: one who mixed a qav of wheat into ten qavim of another's wheat, and the other eats the mixture.
Rav Oshaya comments that the sages were right to mock the one who lost his wheat, as they are laughing at him.
What distinguishes wheat mixed into barley, where the mixture is nullified, from a case of wheat in wheat?
Even wheat in wheat is nullified for the sages, though not for Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that a same-kind mixture is not nullified.
Rav Safra tells Rav Ashi that his explanation is well said.
Objection from a teaching of Rav in the name of Rabbi Chiya: whoever sifts pebbles from another's threshing floor must pay, and Abaye counters with Rav Chisda's rule on carcasses.
The carcass is nullified only when it has no owners, so the rule does not apply to an item that still has an owner.
A baraita of Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri says abandoned objects acquire a resting place even without owners, and Abaye objects that a prohibition cannot be compared to property.
What is the reason for the halakha in the case of dough?
Abaye says the rule is a decree lest one make dough in partnership, so it is not nullified.
Rava says spices are added for their flavor, so their flavor is not nullified in the dough.

39a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Ashi explains that spices, water and salt cannot be nullified because their prohibition is temporary, and temporary prohibitions are never nullified.
The mishna states that Rabbi Yehuda exempts water from the travel limits.
Does this imply that water is exempt but salt is not?
A baraita of Rabbi Yehuda says water and salt are both nullified, so it seems to contradict the mishna.
Resolved: the mishna refers to coarse Sodom salt, which is not nullified, while the baraita refers to fine isteroknit salt.
Another baraita of Rabbi Yehuda says water is nullified in dough but not in a pot, which seems to contradict the mishna.
Resolved: the mishna refers to a thick dish, where water is nullified, and the baraita to a thin dish with liquid sauce.
The mishna teaches that a borrowed coal is as the owner's feet, while a flame may be carried anywhere, with differences in misuse and carrying liability.
A tosefta lists five differences between a coal and a flame: Festival resting place, misuse of consecrated property, idolatry, carrying out, and vows.
What is different about a flame of idol worship, which is permitted, versus consecrated property, which is prohibited, to use?
Idolatry is repulsive, so the Sages did not decree against it, whereas consecrated property is not repulsive and so they decreed a restriction to prevent misuse.
The baraita says one who carries a coal out to the public domain is liable, while one who carries out a flame is exempt.
A baraita says one who carries out a flame of any size is liable, which seems to contradict that ruling.
Rav Sheshet explains the baraita speaks of a flame carried out with a wooden chip attached, which makes the flame significant.
Objection: then the chip itself should create liability, unless the chip is too small to meet the minimum measure for carrying out.
Abaye suggests a vessel smeared with oil and lit, carried out, where the flame is carried on the vessel, which is not a whole vessel but a shard.
Objection: then the shard itself should create liability for carrying out.
The shard must be below the minimum measure, which the mishna of Rabbi Yehuda sets as enough to place between window frames.
If liability arises whenever the flame is attached to a substance, under what circumstances is the mishna's exemption for a flame found?
The flame was fanned by hand into the public domain without being attached to any vessel.
The mishna states that water from a private cistern is as the feet of its owner, water from a town cistern is as the feet of the townspeople, and a public cistern is as the feet of whoever draws it.
Rava raises a contradiction to Rav Naḥman from a tosefta saying water from flowing rivers and springs is as the feet of all people.
Rava explains the mishna refers to collected water, not flowing water, as Shmuel also said.
Amoraim dispute whether, when one fills water from a public cistern for another, the water is as the feet of the one filling it or the one it was filled for.
What is the principle behind this disagreement?
Rav Sheshet holds a public cistern is ownerless so the drawer owns the water, while Rav Naḥman holds it is jointly owned, so the water passes to the one it was drawn for.
Rava challenges Rav Naḥman from a mishna about a ḥerem vow, which prohibits the addressee from benefiting from the speaker.

39b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna rules on ḥerem vows between two parties, and lists which items belong to those coming up from Babylonia and which to a single town.
Rava challenges Rav Naḥman: if a public cistern is jointly owned, the vow-takers should be barred from it, as a mishna in Nedarim teaches.
Rav Naḥman answers that bathing is barred, while the baraita permits only filling water, since each partner's water is retroactively his alone.
Does Rav Naḥman really hold that retroactive designation applies?
A mishna on Shekalim about brothers who divided and rejoined their inheritance seems to show Rav Naḥman rejects retroactive designation.
Rav Anan rules the division is retroactive only if kids and lambs were split evenly, while Rav Naḥman says retroactivity never applies in that case either.
Retracting the earlier explanation, all agree a public cistern is ownerless, and the dispute concerns picking up a found object for a friend.
Rav Naḥman holds a friend acquires a found object picked up on his behalf, while Rav Sheshet holds he does not.
The mishna teaches that produce outside a city's Shabbat limit may not be brought to its owner unless the owner set up an eiruv to that city.

40a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A mishna rules that guests from beyond the Shabbat limit may not carry their gifts home unless the host transferred them before the Festival.
Rav holds that deposited produce is as the feet of the depositary, while Shmuel holds it is as the feet of its owner.
Can we say Rav and Shmuel follow their usual positions on the liability of a homeowner for items brought into his courtyard?
A mishna is cited on liability for items brought into a courtyard, including Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view that the homeowner is not liable unless he accepts the duty to watch them.
Rav Huna reports that Rav held the halakha follows the Rabbis, and Shmuel held it follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
Could Rav's view be in accord with the Rabbis, and Shmuel's with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, in a way that reconciles their positions?
Each amora could have held his view even in accord with the other side, since their positions depend on whether the owner intends the object to be in his jurisdiction.
If deposited produce is as the depositary's feet, what of the mishna's ruling that the owner's eiruv makes it as his own feet?
Rav Huna says the mishna refers to a case where the keeper designated a corner of his house for the owner, so the produce is as the owner's feet.
A second mishna about guests' gifts seems to show that deposited items are not as the depositary's feet, so the reconciliation fails.
Here too, transfer through another person counts as designating a corner, so the gifts are as the guests' feet, or the transfer case differs.
Rav Ḥana bar Ḥanilai hung meat at his host's door outside his town, and Rav Huna ruled he may take it only if he hung it himself.
Objection: Rav Huna was Rav's student, and Rav held deposited items are as the depositary's feet, so the host's meat should follow him.
Rav Ḥana's case differs because he was given a particular spot at the door, which is like designating a corner for him.
Further objections: Shmuel's ox of a fattener, and Rabba bar bar Ḥana's ruling on Rabbi Dosa, and the mishna on animals and vessels, all suggest the meat should be allowed.
The issue is not place of rest but whether the meat was left unobserved, which depends on whether Rav Ḥana himself hung it and kept his attention on it.
The mishna rules that one may water and slaughter domestic animals on a Festival, but not desert animals, which are muktze.
Why does the mishna need to teach watering before slaughter, since it is about which animals may be slaughtered?
The tanna teaches incidentally that one should water the animal before slaughter, since then the skin is easier to remove.
A baraita defines desert animals as those that graze outside the town and enter only at the first rain, and domestic animals as those that sleep within the boundary.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds both kinds are domestic, and only animals that graze outside and never enter settlements in summer or winter are desert.
Does Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi really accept the concept of muktze, given his son's question about unripe dates?
Rabbi Shimon holds there is no recognition of muktze at all, so the question of unripe dates is not a concern.

40b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Muktze applies only to dried figs and raisins in the middle of drying, which were actively removed from use, unlike unripe dates.
Several resolutions: desert animals resemble dried figs, or Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's statement to his son reflects Rabbi Shimon's view, or he spoke for argument's sake against the Rabbis.
A closing formula marks the end of the chapter and of the tractate Beitzah.
